stratcomments: Occurs at the center of the most disrupted strata. Occupies a mini-graben bounded by two parallel SW-NE oriented faults. Sediments produce a pseudochannel. Grading is common.
lithdescript: Horizons vary greatly in degree of texture (siltstones to coarse lapilli tuffs) and degree of induration. In general the coarser and/or more calcareous horizons are more strongly indurated. Grading is common in coarser sections.Grading is common and most evident in the coarser horizons. Upward-fining horizons outnumber upward coarsening horizons, and flame structures occur at the top the coarse lapilli tuff of horizon 2.25. Two horizons near the base of the sequence (1.5 and 1.9) contain abundant in situ pteridosperm roots and can therefore be confidently described as paleosols. Two thick siltstone horizions...contain nodular calcareous concretions. The lower siltstone is a slightly darker grey and richer in pyrite than the upper...

lithdescript: The Coconino Sandstone of teh mid-Permian age is visible at the top of Promnotory Butte and forms white to yellow massive cliffs exhibiting wedges of cross-bedding. This SS grades downward into a continous redbed sequence of siltstone-sandstone, then a limestone interbed, a cross-bedded red siltstone, a calcareous shale that weathers to pebble-sixed fragments with a limonite stain, with the plant horizon 1-3 m thick over a coaly layer.
primary_reference: J. E. Canright. 1978. A Late Paleozoic Flora from Promontory Butte in Central Arizona. Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Vegetation in East-Central Arizona: American Association of Stratigraphic Palynologists 11th Annual Meeting

geogcomments: The Horse Prairie Florule receives its name from the Horse Prairie Basin and Creek near Grant in southwestern Montana. It comprises plant fossils from various sites of identical horizon, mainly along the south side of an east-west highway (324) which leads from the former town of Armstead (now submersed under Clark Canyon Reservoir) over Grant and the Bannack Pass on the Continental Divide, to Leadore in Idaho. This highway parallels a defunct railroad which was formerly used by th elumber and cattle industry. it is almong the embankments of the road and the cuts of the railroad bed that fossiliferous deposits are in evidence. These beds, representing geological sites 66, 93 and 69 (ORR) are exposed for over two miles in a westerly direction. About one half mile west of site 69, a field road leads to geological site 133, one half mile south of the highway. Another fossiliferous outcrop, geological site 70 is located four miles west of Grant, and about 1000 feet along another field road south of the highway. This locality is seperated from the other sites by a fault, but it is assumed to have been contigous. It is know as the Metasequoia-Osmunda site for its abundance of these species, and the lack of any othe rplants. The matrix of this site differs essentially from all others by its interbedded thin layers of coal, lignite, ash and burnt, red clays. Lignites from this and other localities are now under in vestigation for pollen analysis. The location of these outcrops in th emiddle of the old railroad bed precludes tracing or outlining this deposit. but it is probably a lens within the otherwise uniform shales. The individual geological sites are determined as follows from the U.S. Geological Survey. Grant Quadrangle, Beaverhead County, Montana: Site 66 -NW1/4, SW1/4, Sec. 33, T9S, R12W; Site 93- NE1/4, SW1/4,m Sec. 32 T9S, R12W; Site 69- Se1/4, SW1/4, NE1/4 Sec. 31 T9S, R12 W; Site 70- SW1/4, Sec. 35, T9s, R13; Site 133- NW1/4, SW1/4, NE1/4, Sec. 6, T10S, R12W. To the north of teh road, about half of the Beaverhead basins area stretches out in a rather flat expanse becomin ghilly in the distant vicinity of the Christensen Ranch and Bannack the first capital of Montana, and now a ghost town. To the south, starting at the highway near the Horse Prairie outcros, the topography is hilly and gradually rising toward the higher mountains of the Continental Divide which border the entire basin in the southwest. During recent years the highway was "improved", destroying some of the outcrops but most collecting was done prior to that time. The immediate vicinity north of the fossil sites is put to irrigated grazing lands and the production of hay.
primary_reference: H. F. Becker. 1969. Fossil Plants of the Tertiary Beaverhead Basins in Southwestern Montana. Palaeontographica Abteilung B 127:1-142
time_overlap: Aquitanian, Burdigalian, Langhian, Serravallian, Tortonian, Messinian
taxonomy_comments: Becker 1969 gives a composite list for five sites (66, 93, 69, 133, and 70) all within a small area and with fossils collected from "an identical horizon". He only differentiates site 70 because it is particularly sparse (only two taxa) relative to the other sites. He notes that not all the taxa listed occur at all of the remaining sites. Because of this, I've entered Horse Prairie as two collections: one the composite and one for site 70.

geogcomments: The collecting site (USGS paleobotany loc. 10055) is approximately 1 mile northwest of the mouth of Big Moonshine Creek where it becomes an arm of the south side of Lake Kemp in Baylor County. The fossiliferous outcrop was exposed in a low bank 15 feet west of a road that parallels the arm and is about 1/4 mile west of it. The locality is reached by entering the toll gate at Moonshine Colony, 5.6 miles north of Mabelle, on U.S. Highway 183-283, and upon passing the gate, following the main road and the first fork to the south for a total distance of 5.2 miles from the gate to the fossil plant locality. The locality is the property of the W. T. Waggoner Estate.
stratcomments: Extensive rock exposures are rare in this area, and a detailed geologic map of Baylor County is not available. However, there seems to be no doubt that the plant deposit is within the Arroyo Formation. The collecting site is stratigrapically above the Lake Kemp limestone, the uppermost member of the Leuders Formation and thus is an undetermined distance above the bottom of the suberjacent Arroyo Formation. The plants were found in moderate abundance as coalified compressions in a small lens of dark, bluish gray shale, which is badly weathered and friable making removal of fossils difficult. The lens was virtually destroyed by our collecting effors; originally it did not exceet 1 foot in thickness or 5 feet laterally. It was partly capped by a 2 to 6 inch layer of poorly indurated light tan siltstone that contains abundant unidentifiable, coalified plant material intermixed wiht many small bits of bone and teeth. The latter were identified as paleoniscoid fish remains. \r\n\r\nMamay (1986) Siltstone in upper part of the Lueders limestone, Witchita Group, Leonardian
primary_reference: S. H. Mamay. 1967. Lower Permian plants from the Arroyo Formation in Baylor County, north-central Texas. U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 575-C:120-126

collection_aka: USGS paleobotany loc. 10,000\r\nMabelle Limestone of Romer?
geogcomments: The productive outcrop is approximately 6 miles north of Mabelle, in Baylor County, Tex. It is reached by following U.S. Highway 183-283 north from Mabelle to a point 0.4 miles south of the highway bridge under which the Wichita River flows eastward from the spillway of Lake Kemp. At this point one sees a conspicous exposure of predominantly tan sedimentary rocks in a low wast-facing bluff about 125 yards west of the highway; this is the plant-bearing site.
stratcomments: Thus the plants occur near the middle of the Lower Permian which, according to Kummel (1961) and Dutro (1961) is equivalent to the Artinskian interval of the Urals section.
lithdescript: As exposed at this outcrop, the sequence consists of approximately 20 feet of siltstone and sandstone, mostly thin bedded with variable fissility, ranging in color from white to grey, bluish gray or tan and having considerable limonitic streaking. The section is capped by a limestone bed that is light gray in color, ranges from 2 to 3.5 feet in thickness and contains minor amounts of sand. This bed is the only conspicuous limestone in the vicinity of the plant beds and doubtless is the unit mapped my Garrett, Lloyd, and Laskey (1930) as the Mabelle Limestone of Romer (1928) This fossiliferous site will be referred to here as the Lake Kemp Locality (USGS paleobotany loc. 10,000)...Although finely comminuted plant debris is scattered through the entire sequence below the limestone unit, the best preserved plant material was found in a 1-foot unit of tan and blueish-gray siltstone, the base of which is about 5ft above the old roadbed.
primary_reference: S. H. Mamay. 1966. Tinsleya, a new genus of seed-bearing callipterid plants from the Permian of north-central Texas. U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 523-E:1-15

This bed is the only conspicuous limestone in the vicinity of the plant beds and doubtless is the unit mapped my Garrett, Lloyd, and Laskey (1930) as the Mabelle Limestone of Romer (1928) This fossiliferous site will be referred to here as the Lake Kemp Locality (USGS paleobotany loc. 10,000)...Although finely comminuted plant debris is scattered through the entire sequence below the limestone unit, the best preserved plant material was found in a 1-foot unit of tan and blueish-gray siltstone, the base of which is about 5ft above the old roadbed.
geology_comments: The beds in approximately the lower half of the section show minor angular unconformities and discordant bedding planes that suggest a channel-fill type of deposition.

lithdescript: The fossil-bearing unit is about 2m thick and consists of green-grey silty mudstone and conglomerate. Most of the bones lie at the bottom of this unit, whereas the fossil plants are distributed throughout the bed. This unit is underlain by beds of red, purple, and green-hued carbonate, mudstone, fine sandstone, and siltstone. The base of the fossil-bearing unit is incised into the underlying carbonate unit, or even into the oxidized, muddy siltstone beneath the carbonate unit. Bones are often incorporated within lenses of conglomerate consisting of subrounded to rounded carbonate pebbles. Kirkland and Carpenter (1994) interpreted the carbonate pebbles to be transported calcareous soil nodules, but they may be rip-up clasts from the carbonate unit that underlies the fossil bearing unit in some areas.\r\n The fossiliferous unit is overlain by a bed of resistant, fine-grained volcanic tuff which is well cemented and tends to break perpendicular to the bedding. It was from this tuff that one nearly complete articulated fish, and parts of several others, were recovered (see Kirkland, this volume).\r\nThe presence of a laterally continuous carbonate bed below the quarry, and two laterally continuous tuff units above, indicates that the tuffs were deposited in a predominantly lacustrine environment. Based on the lateral extent of the tuffs, it is estimated that the lake was at least 1.5 km wide. The occurrence of articulated fish in the lower tuff unit indicates deposition in quiet water, although the presence of ripple marks suggest that the water was relatively shallow at times. The fact that fossil root casts are present in the tuff to the southwest and east of Rabbit Valley, but absent in the area of the quarry, implies that the lake level receded temporarily, although water remained in the area of the quarry. The disconformable base of the fossiliferous unit which contains lenses of carbonate pebbles and bone, suggests evidence for temporary fluvial conditions when the unit was first being deposited.
primary_reference: W. D. Tidwell, B. B. Britt, and S. R. Ash. 1998. Preliminary floral analysis of the Mygatt-Moore Quarry in the Jurassic Morrison Formation, west-central Colorado. Modern Geology 22:341-378

geogcomments: Collection comes from mainly McClelland's shaft near Belleville, Jasper County, Missouri. Other species in the collection come from the Hannam shaft, 1 mile NE of Carterville, Jasper County, a shaft 1 mile N of Aurora, Lawrence County, from the north end of the Bay State lease near Joplin, Jasper County, and from the Bristow land 4 miles N of Joplin, Jasper County.
lithdescript: Plant materials come from light ash-colored somewhat arenaceous shales with minute particles of mica. Portions are massive, sandy and darker. Black coaly shales.
primary_reference: D. White. 1893. Flora of the Outlying Carboniferous Basins of Southwestern Missouri. United States Geological Survey (98):1-137
lithdescript.1: Plant materials come from light ash-colored somewhat arenaceous shales with minute particles of mica. Portions are massive, sandy and darker. Black coaly shales.
geology_comments: McClelland's Shaft- the basin affects surface topography as a slight sink. Occurs in loose layers of chert brecciated in situ and alternate limestone strata. The bottom of the depression is covered by loose chert. The shales, in a lenticular body, of about 10 feet in thickness very convex below and slightly concave above. At this level the basin iss about thrity feet in diameter.
collection_comments: Collection is from 14 boxes collected by Dr. WP Jenney fot eh USGS in the fall of 1889 during a study of lead and zinc deposits in Missouri.

collection_name: Plants of the Horton Series or Lower Carboniferous Coal Measures
geogcomments: This formation is found in southern Cape Breton, in the county of Sydney, in Hants, at Horton Bluff, at Hillsborough, and other locations in southern New Brunswick.
lithdescript: The Horton Bluff Series or Lower carboniferous Coal-Measures, consisting of hard sandstones and shales often calcareous, associated with conglomerate and grit, and in some places with highly bituminous shales. They contain underclays and thin coaly seams, remains of Plants, Fishes and Entomostracans, and foot-prints of Batrachians, but no strictly marine remains.
primary_reference: J. W. Dawson. 1873. Report on the Fossil Plants of the Lower Carboniferous and Millstone Grit Formations of Canada. Geological Survey of Canada
lithdescript.1: The Horton Bluff Series or Lower carboniferous Coal-Measures, consisting of hard sandstones and shales often calcareous, associated with conglomerate and grit, and in some places with highly bituminous shales. They contain underclays and thin coaly seams, remains of Plants, Fishes and Entomostracans, and foot-prints of Batrachians, but no strictly marine remains.
collection_comments: Sir C. Lyell first established the Horton Bluff Series or Lower Carboniferous Coal-Measures group as a distinct sub-division of the Carboniferous in Nova Scotia. Dawson identifies the following locations as equivalents of the Lower Carboniferous Coal Measures or Horton Series: the Vespertine Group of Rogers in Pennsylvania, the Kinderhook Group of Worthen in Illinois, The Marshall Group of Winchell in Michigan, the Waverley Sandstone of Ohio, the Lower or False Coal Measures of Virginia, the Calciferous Sandstones of McLaren or Tweedian Group of Tate in Scotland, the Carboniferous Slate and Coomhala Grits of Jukes in Ireland, the Culm and Culm Graywacke of Germany, the Graywacke or Lower Coal-Measures of the Vosges,the Older Coal-Formation of the Ural, and the so-called "Ursa Stage" of Heer.

lithdescript.1: The Millstone Grit Series, consisting of sandstones and shales, often red, and conglomerate, associated with dark coloured beds holding fossil plants and Naiadites, and with a few underclays and thin seams of coal.
collection_comments: Mr. R. Brown first used the name Millstone Grit in 1844. In 1843, this group was distinctly indicated in Sir W.E. Logan's section of the South Joggins and in Dawson's paper on the Lower Carboniferous Rocks of Eastern Nova Scotia. Dawson provides the following locations as equivalents of the Millstone Grit Series: the Seral Conglomerate of Rogers in Pennsylvania, the Lower Coal Formation Conglomerate and Chester Groups of Illinois, the Lower Carboniferous Sandstone of Kentucky, Alabama, and Virginia, the Millstone Grit and Yoredale Rocks of Northern England, the Culmiferous of Devonshire, the Moor Rock and Lower Coal Measures of Scotland, the Flagstones and Lower Shales of the South of Ireland and Millstone Grit of the North of Ireland, and the Jungste Graywacke of the Hartz, Saxony, and Silesia.

geogcomments: Upchurch, Crane, & Drinnan (1994) 6444; The Quantico megafloral locality is located at the southern end of the U.S. Marine Corps base at Quantico, Virginia, apporoximatly 30 miles south-west of Washington D.C., and 75 miles north of Richmond, Virginia. The military base is accessed by taking Interstate Highway 95 to the southern exit for the Quantico Marine Base (the first exit south of Triangle, Virginia), then driving east on Russell Road to the south entrance gate. The fossil plant locality is located south of the U.S. Marine Chopawamsic Creek and .5 miles west of the Potomac River. It is located on the south side of Engineers Road, and east-west road running parallel to Chopawamsic Creek. The fossiliferous horizon occurs on the west-facing wall of a gravel pit, which was actively mined in the 1970's, in claybeds exposed approximatly 15 m above the base, near the top of the exposure.

stratcomments: The Winton Formation has yielded spore-pollen assemblages belonging to the Phimopollenites pannosus or succeeding Appendicisporties distocarinatus zone of probable late Albian to Cenomanian age (Dettmann & Playford 1969; Burger, 1970; Morgan, 1980; Helby et al., 1987). Moore & Pitt (1984), on the basis of unpublished palynological data, suggested that the uppermost beds of this formation in central parts of the basin may have been deposited in the late Cenomanian or early Turonian.
lithdescript: Plant fossils are preserved as impressions in buff, pale yellow, dark brown, or pink, siltstones or fine-grained lithic sandstones. Small cross laminae and parallel laminae are evident in the host rocks.
primary_reference: S. McLoughlin, A. N. Drinnan, and A. C. Rozefelds. 1995. A Cenomanian Flora from the Winton Formation, Eromanga Basin, Queensland, Australia. Memoirs of the Queensland Museam 38(1):273-313

geology_comments: Small cross laminae and parallel laminae are evident in the host rocks and together with the relatively undamaged leaf remains and numerous slender invertebrate (?oligochaete) trails, they suggest relatively low enery, ?lacustrine depostional environments.

geogcomments: Specimens occur in mine spoil from the Yangshuling mine in the Pingquan district of Hebei Province, that extracts coals in underground works from the upper part of the Taiyuan Formation.
stratcomments: The Taiyuan formation is considered to be of P1/1 (super and subscript) age in the Chinese stratigraphical system (Tian et al. 1996) correlating with the Asselian-early Sakmarian stages of the Early Permian elsewhere.
lithdescript: Plant compressions are found in several lithologies, including dark grey coloured mudstones, grey coloured fine-grained sandstones and pale grey-yellow seat earth horizons, the latter dominated by poorly preserved and unidentifiable rooting organs.\r\n\r\nPermineralized plant fossils occur in fine-grained grey-green tuff in which the 3D structure and tissue compositions of the plant fossils are preserved. The tuff comprises predominantly sub-angular feldspar crystals in an early stage diagenetic carbonate matrix

geogcomments: 1 km west of Rawley Springs on east side of US rt. 33. A coal bed up to 1.5 m thick rests on a bioturbated and partly rooted mudrock with uneven topography at the top of a fluvial fining upward cycle.
lithdescript: coal bed up to 1.5 m thick rests on a bioturbated and partly rooted mudrock with uneven topography at the top of a fluvial fining upward cycle. Coal is in turn cut by high relief erosion surface of the next cycle above. Within both cycles the erosion surface is overlain by trough cross-stratified hematite cemented sandstones which fine upward into bioturbated and oxidized siltstone and mudstone. Section indicates that plant axes are from base of the sandstone layer.

geogcomments: Fossil localities of Seto-Tajimi region recorded by Miki were as many as 16, and most of them were in teh porcelain clay pits. To collect fossils at some localities is now impossible, because most of clay pits have changed or abandoned their mining sites. [Ozaki] was able to collect leaf fossils from the Itoh Mine in Obata-machi, Toyota City. Obbata, one of Miki's localities seems to correspond tro the Hohtoku Mine area at Ohara of Obata-machi, Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture. Teh Itoh Mine is at the nort of the third pit of the Hohtoku Mine and at the west of teh second pit of the Hohtoku Mine.
stratcomments: The Seto Porcelain Clay Formation around the Itoh and Hohtoku Mines in Obata area is 20 to 30 m thick, which unconformably overlies Mesozoic and Paleogene granitic rocks of large relief and is correlated with the Mizunami Group in Tajimi region by the molluscan fauna.
lithdescript: The Seto Mizunami Group in Tajimi region by the molluscan fauna. The Seto Porcelain Clay Formation in this area is subdivided into three members; the upper and lower members consisting mainly of coarse grained quartz sandstone facies and the middle member of fine grained siltstone facies.

geogcomments: Kimberley, Nottinghamshire. A 20-foot section of Lower Permian Marl is exposed on the south side of the more northerly railway cutting (disused) some 500 yards west of the tunnel at Kimberley, west of Nottingham.
stratcomments: A 4-foot-thick Permian breccia overlies, unconformably, Carboniferous Coal measure Sandstone. The top of the cutting exposes the Lower Magnesium Limestone, which here is arenaceous and gritty, obsuring a clear demarcation between this and the lower Permian marl.

geogcomments: Bay <0.5km NW of Tantallon Castle: 2 exposures, each of single plant-bearing horizon; 1 exposure is low scarp of foreshore, other is at base of GinHead volcanic vent
stratcomments: "cementstone facies overlie the Upper Old Red Sandstone and these comprise a series of sandstones, grey and red mudstones with some calcareous horizions". The sandstones of Canty Bay probably belong to this sequence.
lithdescript: The plant-bearing sediments range from calcareous sandstones to calcareous siltstones and silty limestones (wackestone/packestone). The sandstone is generally poorly bedded and in places contains rounded rip-up clasts mainly of mudstone and siltstone. Rarely, rounded rec ostracod-rich limestone fragments are found which are reminiscent of the Gin Head Shore plant bed and imply a younger geological age.
primary_reference: R. M. Bateman and G. W. Rothwell. 1990. A reappraisal of the Dinantian floras at Oxroad Bay, East Lothian, Scotland. 1. Floristics and the development of whole-plant concepts. Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 81:127-159

geogcomments: The locality from which the fossil plants were obtained is near the northern border of Nebraska, approximately 14 miles from the Nebraska-South Dakota line and 165 miles east of the Nebraska-Wyoming border. It is on the northern border of Cherry County, nearly 22 miles wes of the town of Valentine and 14.5 miles by road south of the town of Kilgore, on the north side (.25 mile from the river) of the Niobrara River Valley. The locality extends along the 2,700 foot contour in the north half of section 34, T. 33 N., R 31 W. in the Kilgore quadrangle of the US Geological Survey, near the west boundary of the Drinkwater Ranch.
lithdescript: the Valentine formation, the lowest member of theOgallala is made up almost entirely of fine gray calcareous sands, with a few horizons of cemented caliche sand. The Valentine rests on an erosion surface developed on rather well cemented sandy or silty clays, dark gray with a pinkish cast. The clay beds have been tentatively assigned to the "Brule Clays" of Oligocene age.
primary_reference: H. D. MacGinitie. 1962. The Kilgore Flora: A Late Miocene Flora from Northern Nebraska. University of California Publications in Geological Sciences 35(2):67-158

geogcomments: Above locality 3VC below locality 3VAL
lithdescript: The sediments of the 3V sequence, and that of most of the Pautut area, are represented mostly as coarsening upward cycles. Tha vary randomly between 2 and 6 meters in thickness. The basal unit of a cycle typically is a thin, not more than 2 cm thick, and horizontally bedded white clay or siltstone sometimes containing closely packed, wood impressions all oriented with a singular lineation.
primary_reference: A. Boyd. 1992. Revision of the Late Cretaceous Pautut Flora from West Greenland: Gymnospermopsida (Cycadales, Cycadeoidales, Caytoniales, Ginkgoales, Coniferales). Palaeontographica Abteilung B 225:105-172
lithdescript.1: The sediments of the 3V sequence, and that of most of the Pautut area, are represented mostly as coarsening upward cycles. Tha vary randomly between 2 and 6 meters in thickness. The basal unit of a cycle typically is a thin, not more than 2 cm thick, and horizontally bedded white clay or siltstone sometimes containing closely packed, wood impressions all oriented with a singular lineation.
geology_comments: This cycle appears to represent a depositional position intermediate between the near shore prodelta and the more basinward bay sediments. These cycles have a thickness and color closer resembling that of teh PRP cycle but with a slightly differnet fossil content. Marine organisms and conifer stems and cones are present but few in number. The angiosperm leaf species represented are the same riparian species as in the near shore cycles but with a greater number of specimens than in those cycles.

geology_comments: Backwater marine bay with a fossil plant assemblage dominated by angiosperm species that, except for a few wide ranging species do no toccur in other fossil horizons at Pautut (PRP) The leaves in these beds appear to be derived mostly from inland levee vegetation. Scheklar et. al. mentined sandstone bodies in the western part of teh marine conditions for these beds. This is supported by the presence of leaves in the PRP beds with encrusting bryozoan species closely related to modern species that occupy brackish water conditions. However the number of other fully marine species in teh PRP and other Pautut beds indicates fluctuating salinities within the basin.

lithdescript: The coarse, lens-enclosing sandstone is about 150 ft. thick and overlain by weakly consolidated gravels. It contains numberous small, non-fossiliferous clay or silt pockets, is distinctly cross-bedded at low angles and the only outcrop of this kind in the Fossil Basin. Generally weakly consolidated, the sandstone is packed, however, forming several resistant low ledges, iron-cemented and rust-stained. Mild rain and melting snow is usually redily absorbed by the remaining sandstone. Both, the angular grains of the sandstone and the mica flakes of the lens, suggest a short distance of transportation for the sediments

geogcomments: The Christensen Ranch Florule (geological sites 32 and 32L, ORR) is located in the southernmost drainage of Grasshopper Creek near Bannack, comprising plant fossils from two small sites at the same locality, but at borizons seperated by about 20 feet of non-fossiliferous rock. The hill on which this florule is located represents one of several island outcrops within the Grasshopper Basin between Resevoir and Buffalo Creeks, and one mile west of the Christensen Rance (SW1/4, NE1/4, Sec. 7, T8S, R12W, Grant Quadrangle, Beaverhead County, Montana). Surrounding areas form a part of the grazing lands, which, to the west abut the Bighole Divide of the Beaverhead Natinoal Forest.

geogcomments: The Horse Prairie Florule receives its name from the Horse Prairie Basin and Creek near Grant in southwestern Montana. It comprises plant fossils from various sites of identical horizon, mainly along the south side of an east-west highway (324) which leads from the former town of Armstead (now submersed under Clark Canyon Reservoir) over Grant and the Bannack Pass on the Continental Divide, to Leadore in Idaho. This highway parallels a defunct railroad which was formerly used by th elumber and cattle industry. it is almong the embankments of the road and the cuts of the railroad bed that fossiliferous deposits are in evidence. These beds, representing geological sites 66, 93 and 69 (ORR) are exposed for over two miles in a westerly direction. About one half mile west of site 69, a field road leads to geological site 133, one half mile south of the highway. Another fossiliferous outcrop, geological site 70 is located four miles west of Grant, and about 1000 feet along another field road south of the highway. This locality is seperated from the other sites by a fault, but it is assumed to have been contigous. It is know as the Metasequoia-Osmunda site for its abundance of these species, and the lack of any othe rplants. The matrix of this site differs essentially from all others by its interbedded thin layers of coal, lignite, ash and burnt, red clays. Lignites from this and other localities are now under in vestigation for pollen analysis. The location of these outcrops in th emiddle of the old railroad bed precludes tracing or outlining this deposit. but it is probably a lens within the otherwise uniform shales. The individual geological sites are determined as follows from the U.S. Geological Survey. Grant Quadrangle, Beaverhead County, Montana: Site 66 -NW1/4, SW1/4, Sec. 33, T9S, R12W; Site 93- NE1/4, SW1/4,m Sec. 32 T9S, R12W; Site 69- Se1/4, SW1/4, NE1/4 Sec. 31 T9S, R12 W; Site 70- SW1/4, Sec. 35, T9s, R13; Site 133- NW1/4, SW1/4, NE1/4, Sec. 6, T10S, R12W. To the north of teh road, about half of the Beaverhead basins area stretches out in a rather flat expanse becomin ghilly in the distant vicinity of the Christensen Ranch and Bannack the first capital of Montana, and now a ghost town. To the south, starting at the highway near the Horse Prairie outcros, the topography is hilly and gradually rising toward the higher mountains of the Continental Divide which border the entire basin in the southwest. During recent years the highway was "improved", destroying some of the outcrops but most collecting was done prior to that time. The immediate vicinity north of the fossil sites is put to irrigated grazing lands and the production of hay.

taxonomy_comments: Becker 1969 gives a composite list for five sites (66, 93, 69, 133, and 70) all within a small area and with fossils collected from "an identical horizon". He only differentiates site 70 because it is particularly sparse (only two taxa) relative to the other sites. He notes that not all the taxa listed occur at all of the remaining sites. Because of this, I've entered Horse Prairie as two collections: one the composite and one for site 70.

geogcomments: The Medicine Lodge Florule is the youngest and stratigraphically the uppermost of the units within the fossiliferous beds of the Beaverhead Basins flora in a larger sense, and of its subsidiary Medicine Lodge Creek Basin particularly. For purposes of uniformity in the areal descriptino of teh ancient basin, this southern valley will also be considered an integral part of the Beaverhead Basins, while geographically the Medicine Lodge Creek dominates the valley. Drainage from the western Idaho Range and numerous tributaries. The northern boundry of the Medicine Lodge Valley is along the Armstead-Leadore-Lemhi road, parallel to the Horse Prairie hills and outcrops. In its length of 18 miles, the valley narrows considerably toward the south, terminating at Medicine Lodge Pass. As a part of teh larger Missouri River drainage system, the Medicine Lodge Creek enters the Horse Prairie Creek just east of Grant, which, in turn joins the Beaverhead River near the easter embayment of Clark Canyon Reservoir (formerly the site fo Armstead). A ranch road, which roughly parallels the Butte-Salt Lake City highway (91) about 20 to 25 miles west across teh Tendoy Mountais, begins jsut east of Grant, bisects the sites of teh florule, and terminates at Dubois, Idaho. The proximity of mountains, the rising elevation of teh narrowing valley, and a large number of small streams furnish sufficient moisture for limited cattle and sheep ranching.\r\n The Medicine Lodge florule consists of three extensive fossiliferous sites in proximity to each other, collectively representing the geological type section 155 (OOR) of the as yet unnamed formation (ORR). Each fossil site is located along a bluff above a creek, all within a short distance from the road, and seperated from each othe ronly by Recent erosioni of the benches which onece formed a contiguous unit. In this way the fossil sites are easily identifiable as the Anton Creek locality with 55 species, about two miles west of the road (Sec. 27, 28, T11S, R12W); the Schwartz Creek locality (geol. site 155/302) with 44 species, about one half mile west of the road (Sec. 26, 27, T11S, R12W); and the Johnson Creek locality (geol. site 155/213) with 31 species, about one half mile east of the road (Sec. 118, T11S, R11W). These small, but premanent creeeks enter the Medicine Lodge Creek within one half mile of each other.

Each fossil site is located along a bluff above a creek, all within a short distance from the road, and seperated from each othe ronly by Recent erosioni of the benches which onece formed a contiguous unit. In this way the fossil sites are easily identifiable as the Anton Creek locality with 55 species, about two miles west of the road (Sec. 27, 28, T11S, R12W); the Schwartz Creek locality (geol. site 155/302) with 44 species, about one half mile west of the road (Sec. 26, 27, T11S, R12W); and the Johnson Creek locality (geol. site 155/213) with 31 species, about one half mile east of the road (Sec. 118, T11S, R11W). These small, but premanent creeeks enter the Medicine Lodge Creek within one half mile of each other.

geogcomments: vicinity of Stonesfield village, 17km NW of Oxford
lithdescript: The fossiliferous tilestones known as the Stonesfield Slate....are of variable lithology, ranging from calcareous sandstone to siltstone, with impersistent oolitic laminae. They have a characteristic fine, horizontal lamination that allowed the splitting of the 'slates'.
primary_reference: C. J. Cleal and P. M. Rees. 2003. The Middle Jurassic flora from Stonesfield, Oxfordshire, UK. Palaeontology 46(4):739-801
lithdescript.1: The fossiliferous tilestones known as the Stonesfield Slate....are of variable lithology, ranging from calcareous sandstone to siltstone, with impersistent oolitic laminae. They have a characteristic fine, horizontal lamination that allowed the splitting of the 'slates'.
collection_comments: The original material was mostly obtained from underground mine workings that closed around a century ago, so the museum specimens are what remains (mostly housed in the NHM, London, and Oxford University Museum).

collection_name: Korpad formation borehole M1 Mecsek Mountains Hungary
geogcomments: samples of the Korpad Formation (Po 306 and 1216) were obtained from borehole M1 (depth 86-87m)core, located near Gyurufu in the western part of the Mecsek Mountains \r\n
stratcomments: This is built up by clastic rocks of predominantly red colour, but green and grey sandstones, too, occur frequently in it. Frequency of burrowing organisms is a characteristic feature of the reddisch brown, siltic, fine grained sandstones which close the cycle.
lithdescript: This is built up by clastic rocks of predominantly red colour, but green and grey sandstones, too, occur frequently in it. Frequency of burrowing organisms is a characteristic feature of the reddisch brown, siltic, fine grained sandstones which close the cycle.
primary_reference: A. Barabas-Stuhl. 1981. Microflora of the Permian and Lower Triassic sediments of the Mecsek Mountains (south Hungary). Acta Geologica Academiae Scientarum Hungaricae 24(1):49-97
time_overlap: Asselian, Sakmarian, Artinskian, Kungurian, Roadian, Wordian, Capitanian, Wuchiapingian, Changhsingian
lithdescript.1: This is built up by clastic rocks of predominantly red colour, but green and grey sandstones, too, occur frequently in it. Frequency of burrowing organisms is a characteristic feature of the reddisch brown, siltic, fine grained sandstones which close the cycle.
geology_comments: The Korpad sandstone formation rests disconformably on Precambrian granites. On the uneven surface of the Korpad Sandstone formation the Gyurufu Quartzporphyry formation rests with a low angle disconformity.
taxonomy_comments: ref. 6870: The poor macroflora collected from this formation has been determined by G. Andreanszky (1961) as follows: Voltzia heterophylla Brgt., Pecopteris sp.. Presence of Voltzia heterophylla is, however, ambigous as this species is characteristic for the higher beds of the Lower Triassic. \r\nNote - The article on which these comments are based are not found in the reference list.

The locations of the mines that provided the flora are as follows:
 Long and Price Mine....SW1/4, NE1/4, sec. 7, T. 8 N., R. 5 W.
 Hannum Mine............NE1/2 SE1/4 sec. 7, T. 8 N., R. 5 W.
 Ray Mine...............NE1/4 SW1/4 sec. 7, T. 8 N., R. 5 W.
 Michaels Mine..........E1/2 SW1/4 sec. 12, T. 8 N., R. 6 W.
The Long and Price, Hannum, and Ray sites were strip mines in which the Lower Block Coal had been removed. The Michaels Mine, from which only a small amount of fossil material was obtained, was also a strip mine, but it yielded both Lower Block Coal and Upper Block Coal. Because the Lower Block Coal was the last coal obtained from the Michaels Mine, the spoil banks were topped by the overburden which had been above the Lower Block Coal, and it was from this material that the ironstone concretions were obtained.

collection_name: Flowerpot Fm. Blaine Beckham Greer Kiowa Major Woods Woodward Oklahoma
geogcomments: Pollen and spores have been recovered from the upper 10-35 feet of the flowerpot Formation of western Oklahoma. Samples are from 46 localities in four counties (Woods, Woodward, Major, Blaine) of North central Oklahoma and three counties (Beckham, Greer, Kiowa) of southwestern Oklahoma. The strata from which sporomorphs have been recoveried lie at the top of the formation, including horizons E through I of Fay (1964) in north central Oklahoma and the interval from the Kiser Gypsum Member to the top of the formation in the southwestern part of the state.\r\n
stratcomments: Red shales and silts are the predominant lithologies, but red sasds, greenisch shales and silts, and, toward the top of the formation, dark-bluish and black shales, dolomites, gypsums, and gypsum stringers are not uncommon.
lithdescript: toward the top of the formation, dark-bluish and black shales
primary_reference: W.B. Clapham. 1970. Permian miospores from the Flowerpot Formation of western Oklahoma. Micropaleontology 16(1):15-36
lithdescript.1: toward the top of the formation, dark-bluish and black shales
geology_comments: The Flowerpot Fm. is a brackisch water to marine red-bed formation interfingering with the continental Chickasha Formation. The formation is bounded above by the medicine Lodge gypsum Member of the highly gypsiferous Blaine formation and below by the Hennessey Formation.

collection_name: Platy Dolomite Ca3 Tumlin-Podgrodzie IG1 borehole Kielce
geogcomments: Sample taken from borehole Tumlin-Podgrodzie IG1 located about 10 km north of Kielce.
stratcomments: The following lithological complexes are currently distinguished within the Zechstein on the so-called "near" Permian-Mesozoic edge of the Holy Cross Paleozoic core: Zechstein Limestone (Ca1) locally underlaying by the Copper-Bearing Shale (in German Kupfer schiefer; T1), Lower Anhydrite (Ald) in some sections, Terrigenious Series (T1r) and Upper Anhydrite (A1g) which all form the Werra Cycle (PZ1); the Strassfort Cycle (PZ2) is developed as the Terrigenous Series (T2r), the Grey Pelite (T3), Platy Dolomite (Ca3) and only locally Main Anhydrite (A3) represents the Leine Cycle (PZ3). The uppermost Zechstein deposits consist of the Top Terrigenous Series (Pzt).
lithdescript: in text: it occurs there in the form of the algal limestones with a mixture of bioclasts. In the northern subregion deposits are thicker (up to 10 m) and bipartate: algal bioloites at the bottom are overlain by the alternating micrite and marl layers.\r\n\r\nin log: dolomites and laminated limestones
primary_reference: A. Fijalkowska. 1994. Palynological aspects of the Permo-Triassic succession in the Holy Cross Mountains, Poland. Documenta Naturae 87:1-76

collection_name: Zechstein Limestone Ca1-d Jaworze IG1 borehole Poland
geogcomments: Sample taken from borehole Jaworze IG1 located about 10 km north of Kielce.
stratcomments: The following lithological complexes are currently distinguished within the Zechstein on the so-called "near" Permian-Mesozoic edge of the Holy Cross Paleozoic core: Zechstein Limestone (Ca1) locally underlaying by the Copper-Bearing Shale (in German Kupfer schiefer; T1), Lower Anhydrite (Ald) in some sections, Terrigenious Series (T1r) and Upper Anhydrite (A1g) which all form the Werra Cycle (PZ1); the Strassfort Cycle (PZ2) is developed as the Terrigenous Series (T2r), the Grey Pelite (T3), Platy Dolomite (Ca3) and only locally Main Anhydrite (A3) represents the Leine Cycle (PZ3). The uppermost Zechstein deposits consist of the Top Terrigenous Series (Pzt).
lithdescript: in text: micritic, oolitic limestones and dolomites and marls\r\nin log: limestones and oolithic limestones, silty limestones or dolomites
primary_reference: A. Fijalkowska. 1994. Palynological aspects of the Permo-Triassic succession in the Holy Cross Mountains, Poland. Documenta Naturae 87:1-76

collection_name: Upper Anhydrite A1g-b Jaworze IG1 borehole Kielce
geogcomments: Sample taken from borehole Jaworze IG1 located about 10 km north of Kielce.
stratcomments: The following lithological complexes are currently distinguished within the Zechstein on the so-called "near" Permian-Mesozoic edge of the Holy Cross Paleozoic core: Zechstein Limestone (Ca1) locally underlaying by the Copper-Bearing Shale (in German Kupfer schiefer; T1), Lower Anhydrite (Ald) in some sections, Terrigenious Series (T1r) and Upper Anhydrite (A1g) which all form the Werra Cycle (PZ1); the Strassfort Cycle (PZ2) is developed as the Terrigenous Series (T2r), the Grey Pelite (T3), Platy Dolomite (Ca3) and only locally Main Anhydrite (A3) represents the Leine Cycle (PZ3). The uppermost Zechstein deposits consist of the Top Terrigenous Series (Pzt).
lithdescript: In text: In the top part of the PZ1 cycle there are sulphate rocks which correspond to the Upper Anhydrite. The thickness varies from 2 to 28 m. In the majority of boreholes this series is bipartate, divided by thin, several meters thick layers of brown claystones and mudstones. Its lower part is composed of anhydrites laminated with clay, the upper one is dominated by sulphates. Equivalents of these rocks are mudstones with the thin layers of algal limestones in the southern subregion. In these deposits there is also a sedimentary breccia corresponding most probably to the Upper Anhydrite Breccia (BrA1g).
primary_reference: A. Fijalkowska. 1994. Palynological aspects of the Permo-Triassic succession in the Holy Cross Mountains, Poland. Documenta Naturae 87:1-76
lithdescript.1: In text: In the top part of the PZ1 cycle there are sulphate rocks which correspond to the Upper Anhydrite. The thickness varies from 2 to 28 m. Its lower part is composed of anhydrites laminated with clay, the upper one is dominated by sulphates. Equivalents of these rocks are mudstones with the thin layers of algal limestones in the southern subregion. In these deposits there is also a sedimentary breccia corresponding most probably to the Upper Anhydrite Breccia (BrA1g).
geology_comments: The Holy Cross Mountains belonged to the costal zone of he Germanic basin during the Late Permian and Upper Triassic. Therefore some members of the Zechstein and Buntsandstein lithological sections are missing or reduced in comparison to the deeper part of the basin.

geogcomments: NW 1/4 NW 1/4 NW 1/4 Sec. 19, T. 17 N., R. 9 W. It lies at a road intersection but a few feet east of the Blaine County line.
stratcomments: K-1 specimens in Olson (1965) are referred to as "Chickasha Formation, middle Flowerpot age, Upper Permian." The terms Flowerpot and Chickasha Formations are historically used interchangeably Olson and Barghusen (1962).\nMinimum age originally entered as >> Capitanian <<. These beds, however, are likely to be older (see, e.g., Reisz & Laurin, 2002, 114(9)).
lithdescript:
"The bone-bearing sediments form a mass with a lenticular cross section, about ten feet across." I - VI are listed top to bottom.
I. Brown to red sandy shale containing a few bones and some plant remains.
II. Fine, soft, brown sandstone with scattered clay pebbles. Grading into green sandstone in places and becoming hard in vicinity of bones. Source of better preserved specimens.
III. Hard brown to red conglomerate. Matrix a mixture of sand and shale, larger constituents include clay pebbles, sandstone pebbles, and small cobbles. Contains scattered fragments of bone and traces of plants.
IV. Rounded and angular fragments of shale and sandstone in a fine, hard matrix forming a conglomerate and breccia. Red to deep brown in color and in part cemented by silica. Bone fragments, well-preserved ribs, and plant remains present.
V. Soft green sandstone with few bones but abundant plant remains, some fairly well preserved.
VI. Green shale with some sand. Plant remains but no bones.
primary_reference: E. C. Olson and H. Barghusen. 1962. Permian vertebrates from Oklahoma and Texas.  Part I.—Vertebrates from the Flowerpot Formation, Permian of Oklahoma. Oklahoma Geological Survey, Circular 59:5-48

geogcomments: La Cierva township, 20 km E of Cuenca, in the Castellana Branch of the Iberian Range
stratcomments: also called "Calizas de La Huérgina Formation" or "La Huérgina Limestones Formations"
lithdescript: Limestone with laminates; three facies described: Massive limestone, packstones with peloids and sand-sized fragments of Charophyte stems. Occasionally, in the base of these beds, levels of gastropodal wackestones appear; Flaggy limestones, sometimes nodular. Ostracodal mudstones with occasional thick laminations, laterally grading to confolute laminations; Laminated limestones, mudstones with laminations containing abundant fossils. Laminae are very continuous laterally
primary_reference: J. L. Sanz, S. Wenz, and A. Yebenes, R. Estes, X. Martinez-Delclos, E. Jiminez-Fuentes, C. Dieguez, A. D. Buscalioni, L. J. Barbadillo, L. Via. 1988. An Early Cretaceous faunal and floral continental assemblage: Las Hoyas fossil site (Cuenca, Spain). Géobios 21(5):611-635
lithdescript.1: Limestone with laminates; three facies described: Massive limestone, packstones with peloids and sand-sized fragments of Charophyte stems. Occasionally, in the base of these beds, levels of gastropodal wackestones appear; Flaggy limestones, sometimes nodular. Ostracodal mudstones with occasional thick laminations, laterally grading to confolute laminations; Laminated limestones, mudstones with laminations containing abundant fossils. Laminae are very continuous laterally
geology_comments: shallow to deep lacustrine facies; "produced in the context of a continental (freshwater) subtropical, seasonal summer wet, carbonate wetland that overlay a low-relief karstic terrain.  The wetland was drained by carbonate-rich freshwater and comprised a typical environmental mosaic of swampy plains, ponds, lakes, ephemeral channels and sloughs."
collection_comments: Repository: Museo de las Ciencias de Castilla-La Mancha, Cuenca (MCCM)

lithdescript: The two beds at Brueckelholz are a "Sandy Coal" which appears intercalated with a coal bed and overlain by sands which contain the second "flora" reported in this paper. No mention of colors are made in the text. I remember the sands as light in color.

geology_comments: Fossils are recovered from a small river within the "Ur-Naab" drainage. This is incised into Triassic bedrock. The channels are a few 10s of meters deep and 1-2 km wide. The Brueckelholz channel includes pure sands, coals, mixed sands and coals, and "paper-thin, grey, diatomaceous, leaf coals" bespeaking great changes in flow regime.

lithdescript: Miocene clays occur in the south-eastern part of the outcrop, which is 8 m. high; marine clays occur at the bottom, freshwater ones at the top, and there is also a passage layer of brackish character..... The flora was collected mainly from the freshwater bed...., partly also from the brackish one.
primary_reference: W Szafer. 1961. Miocenska Flora ze Starych Gliwic na Slasku (Miocene Flora of Stare Gliwice in Upper Silesia). Prace Instytut Geologiczny 33:1-205

geogcomments: Desert Lake Quadrangle
stratcomments:
Kirkland et al. 2016 stated that Tempskya are only known from the Mussentuchit Member within the Cedar Mountain Formation. This is recently believed to be Cenomanian in age according to Tucker et al. 2020.

A radiometric age of 98.37 ± 0.07 Ma was obtained by the OMNH from volcanic ash within the Mussentuchit Member (Cifelli and others,  1997,  1999).  Additional  ages  by  Garrison  and  others (2007)  ranging from 96.7 ± 0.5 to 98.2 ±0.6 Ma indicate  that  the  Mussentuchit  Member  was  deposited  over an interval of 1.5 Ma during the early Cenomanian and  supports  a  correlation  with  the  siliceous  marine  Mowry  Shale  to  the  north,  which  is  well-constrained  from 40Ar/39Ar  sanidine  ages  obtained  from  bentonite  beds that bracket the Mowry in Wyoming; the basal Arrow Creek Bentonite is 98.5 ± 0.5 Ma and the capping Clay Spur Bentonite is 97.2 ± 0.7 Ma (Obradovich, 1993; Ogg and  Hinnov, 2012; Sprinkel and others, 2012) near the base of the Upper Cretaceous. Tucker et al. 2020 also suggested a likely depositional age of ~96-94Ma for the Musseuntuchit member.

stratcomments: The Glen Rose formation spans through four ammonite zones with ages between latest Aptian and early Albian. Young 1974 suggested the Kasanskyella spathi ammonite zone is latest aptian, the Hypacanthoplites cragini zone is earliest Albian, the Douvilleiceras mammillatum and Hypacanthoplites comalensis zones are early Albian and may extend into the middle Albian. The benthic foraminifera Orbitolina texana also suggests a late aptian - early albian age and is found in basal levels and in the upper member (Stricklin et al. 1971). Scott et al. (2007) estimated that the age of the Glen Rose Formation ranges from 113.3 to 108.0 Ma.
primary_reference: J. Watson and H. L. Fisher. 1984. A new conifer genus from the Lower Cretaceous Glen Rose Formation, Texas. Palaeontology 27(4):719-727
collection_comments: The taxa have been redescribed, which were first described by Fontaine, W.M. 1893. Notes on some fossil plants from the Trinity Division of the Comanche Series of Texas. Proc. Nat. Mus. 16, 261-282

geogcomments: Outcrop located on the Graitery anticline on the eastern side of the Gorge de Court.
stratcomments: Röschenz Beds formerly known as the Natica Beds (Gygi, 1995)\r\nthe deposits from which the flora was collected are situated in a facies transition from the Günsberg to Röschenz Beds.
lithdescript: Detrital quartz grains and mud cracks present.\r\nDeposits are entirely marine with mainly oolites and pellets in the lower half of the section and marly, lagoonal limestones, containing red oncolites and bioclasts (mainly large gastropods) in the upper half). The material was collected from this facies transition.\r\n
primary_reference: R. Allenbach and J.H.A. van Konijnenburg-van Cittert. 1997. On a small flora with Araucariaceous conifers from the Röschenz Beds of Court, Jura Mountains, Switzerland. Eclogae geol. Helv. 90:571-579

lithdescript: This Jurassic series: 10m of sandstone overlain by about 4m of silt and clay with the flora. Above these 27m sandstone with silty intercalation follow which end in an irregular ferruginous surface. Above about 70m usually massive in part reddish to purplish sandstones follow with their top formed by an up to 4m thick baltic sill.

collection_name: Heilgersdorf clay layer and overlying sandstone, Sesslach, Coburg
geogcomments: Quarry located at Heilgersdorf, near Coburg (Germany), Germanic basin.
stratcomments: Rhaetian succession overlain by marine Liassic beds.
lithdescript: The base of the quarry consists of several metres of sandstone (Rhät Hauptsandstein). Above this sandstone: Rhät Hauptton, consisting of several layers of clay with some intercalated lenticular coals seams up to 15 cm thick, followed by a sandstone layer ("Oberer Sandstein"). The main plant bed is found in the basal "Hauptton" (1) which is 1-2m thick. Plant remains have also been found in the basal overlying sandstone (2), including Lepidopteris.\r\n
primary_reference: K.-P. Kelber and J.H.A. van Konijnenburg-van Cittert. 1997. A new Rhaetian flora from the neighbourhood of Coburg (Germany) - preliminary results. Proceedings 4th EPPC 58:105-114

geogcomments: 28 locations were studied in the Causses Basin
stratcomments: The Calcaires à stipites is located underneath the Dolomies ruiniformes layer and above a regional unconformities which lies atop of shallow water marine limestones
lithdescript: The limestone beds between the lignite layers are either shallow to marginal marine, lacustrine or palustrine. Lignite beds and associated clays have preserved freshwater flora.
primary_reference: M. Philippe, F. Thevenard, and G. Barale, S. Ferry, G. Guignard. 1998. Middle Bathonian floras and phytocoenoses of France. Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology 143:135-158
lithdescript.1: The limestone beds between the lignite layers are either shallow to marginal marine, lacustrine or palustrine. Lignite beds and associated clays have preserved freshwater flora.
geology_comments: The lignite-bearing unit is made up of thin depositional cycles whose thickness may reach ten metres or so, but usually is much less, sometimes only several decimetres. The thinnest sequences are composed of a transgressive lignite overlain by subaerial palustrine limestones bioturbated by roots.
taxonomy_comments: The palynological data from the Causses Basin is studied twice (Causses 1 and Causses 2). Once (Causses 1) by Doubinger (1961) and once by Alabouvette (1988) (Causses 2).\r\n\r\nThe megaflora data comes partly from Saporta (1873 and 1891), Maubeuge (1949), Gérard (1936), Nickles (1907), Lemoigne (1968) and new data by authors.

taxonomy_comments:
Material mostly studied by others, here reviewed and grouped.

There are no palynological data available from Mamers. The palynological data found in Champlitte (other collection with this reference) by Médus and Mojon (1996) is thought to be a good approximation.

The megaflora data is partly derived from Lignier (1911) and partly is described by Philippe et al. (1998)

collection_name: Ankozany, Sakamena sediments of the Majunga Basin, Madagascar Early Triassic
geogcomments:
Karoo deposits, Majunga Basin ( Andreba area), northern Madagascar
During the interval Late Carbonifirous – Early Jurassic, Madagascar occupied a position to the North opposite Tanzania. 
The section is exposed at an east facing escarpment and exhibits the unconformity between Sakamena sediments and the coarse sandstone of the Isalo.
The Karoo sediments crop out in a relatively narrow belt which extends from the Sakoa area in the South to the Barabanja area in the north of the island.
Material comes from Andrianambo section, located 2 km west of Ankozany 
Plant microfossils have been recovered from the lowermost 4 meters of the Andrianambo section.
stratcomments: Stage: Nammalian = Induan = Olenekian = Smithian = Dienerian\r\n
primary_reference: O. Hankel. 1993. Early Triassic plant microfossils from Sakamena sediments of the Majunga Basin, Madagascar. Review of Palaeobotany and Palynology 77:213-233
geology_comments: From Early Permian times onwards, continental sedimentation was repeatedly influenced or interrupted by marine ingressions documented by the presence of brackish water horizons and shallow marine deposits.\r\nThe lower and middle part of the Sakamena section is a black argillaceous shale which contains nodules and a few thin sandstone beds. Above an unexposed interval a grey sandy shale occurs immediately below the Isalo sandstone.\r\nDeposition of the Sakamena shale occurred probably in a lagoonal or tidal flat environment.

stratcomments:
Kirkland et al. 2016 stated that Tempskya are only known from the Mussentuchit Member within the Cedar Mountain Formation. This is recently believed to be Cenomanian in age according to Tucker et al. 2020.

A radiometric age of 98.37 ± 0.07 Ma was obtained by the OMNH from volcanic ash within the Mussentuchit Member (Cifelli and others,  1997,  1999).  Additional  ages  by  Garrison  and  others (2007)  ranging from 96.7 ± 0.5 to 98.2 ±0.6 Ma indicate  that  the  Mussentuchit  Member  was  deposited  over an interval of 1.5 Ma during the early Cenomanian and  supports  a  correlation  with  the  siliceous  marine  Mowry  Shale  to  the  north,  which  is  well-constrained  from 40Ar/39Ar  sanidine  ages  obtained  from  bentonite  beds that bracket the Mowry in Wyoming; the basal Arrow Creek Bentonite is 98.5 ± 0.5 Ma and the capping Clay Spur Bentonite is 97.2 ± 0.7 Ma (Obradovich, 1993; Ogg and  Hinnov, 2012; Sprinkel and others, 2012) near the base of the Upper Cretaceous. Tucker et al. 2020 also suggested a likely depositional age of ~96-94Ma for the Musseuntuchit member.

Relatively shallow marine environment where ecological conditions were not conductive to the development of an extensive lycopsid-sphenopsid-filicinean flora, and the dominant floral elements seem to have been of upland types.

Other ecological interpretations of Wellington Formation by other authors:
Shaffer (1964) studied the middle portion of the Wellington Formation (Hutchinson Salt Member, Rice and Reno Counties, Kansas): two ecological contrasting floral realms: mesic lowlands and upland areas.
Hedlund (1965) also studied the Wellington Formation (135 miles south of Kansas locaties of Shaffer): swamp-type floras/marginal swamp environment.

The assemblage from Bond is located midway between the localities of Shaffer and Hedlund.

collection_name: Permian Bolzano Volcanic Complex, Southern Italy
geogcomments:
In the central Southern Alps ( Alto Adige/ South Tyrol; northern Italy.
The study area is located in the Bolzano graben system, the Bolzano Volcanic Complex is superjacent to the Variscan basement.

Four sections have been investigated. These four section were located at Grissian Georde, Gorl ( two sections) and Oberbozen.

The Permian succession consist of two tectono-sedimentary cycles. 
The first involves infilling of small intermontane grabens, or half-grabens and is dominated by alluvial fan and lacustrine sediments and volcanics.
The second cycle, which begins above a marked unconformity, consists of fluvial, coastal sabkha and shallow marine deposits. These cover the sediments of the lower tectono-sedimentary cycle and the structural highs in between.
The Bolzano Volcanic complex belongs to the lower cycle and reaches a maximum thickness of approximately 3 km, and a areal extent of 4,000 km², including an area covered by Mesozoic sediments.
stratcomments: The Gröden Formation, which overlies the Bolzano Volcanic Complex, has yielded a wealth of paleontological and biostratigraphical information.(Palynomorphs, tetrapod footpronts, and a marine fauna which includes orthocone nautiloids.) and is aged at Midian – Dzhulfian ( Late Permian )
lithdescript:
The Bolzano Volcanic Complex sequence consists primarily of ignimbrites, pyroclastics and subordinate rhyodacitic lava flows and andesitic rocks. 
The succession can be roughly divided into a lower group dominated by andesitic to dacitic-rhyodacitic volcanic rocks and an upper group consisting of rhyodacitic to rhyolithic volcanic rocks.
Inter volcanic sediments including silica layers inetrcalate with stromatolitic carbonates, sandstones, siltstones and mudstones. They are interpreted as fluvial lacustrine sediments deposite during volcanic quiescence. Clastic sediments containing weathered volcanic rock transported to small basins formed by volcanotectonic processes within the Bolzan Volcanic Complex are the result of sheet floods and debris flows.
The precence of soft-sediment deformation structures, shrinkage features and pristine three-dimensionally preserved palynomorphs suggests very early diagenetic precipitation and consolidation prior to mechanical compaction of sediment.
primary_reference: C. Hartkopf-Fröder, G. D. Wood, and K. Krainer. 2001. Palynology of the Permian Bolzano Volcanic Complex, Southern Alps, Italie, part 1: miospore preservation, quantitative spore color and quantitative fluorescene microscopy. American Association of Stratigraphic Palynologists Foundation

stratcomments:
The Buntsandstein strate studied belong to the Tabuenca-Rodanas alienation, i.e the Aragonian branch northern edge of the Iberian Range.

taxonomy_comments: Macro- and microfloral assemblages are dominated by conifer remains. The microflora are, in this respect, perfectly consistent with the macroflora.

lithdescript: Trough cross-bedded sandstone, gravely sandstone and fine-grained conglomerate. It commonly shows lenticular geometry and an erosional base. In most cases it consists of medium to coarse-grained sandstone, occasionally with sparse granules and small pebbles; trough cross-bedded conglomerates were only observed in section 18. Thickness of through cross-bedded units average 65 cm and ranges 20-180 cm. Set height is usually less than 20 cm. Isolated units typically occur as shallow lenticular bodies fining upwards from coarse to medium or fine sandstone, and usually encased within siltstone or sandy/gravely mudstone; they commonly occur as composite units consisting of a number of mutually erosive sets, locally with mud drapes on the troughs, associated in places with planar lamination. Liquefraction pockets are locally observed.

stratcomments: Val Gardena Sandstone in the Bletterbach section was regarded as Uppermost Capitanian-Dzhulfian in age, while the Bellerophron formation was attributed to the Dorashamian-Changxingian.
lithdescript:
The Upper Permian deposits of the eastern Southern Alps display the typical features of early rift successions: onset of sedimentation after a long period of subaerial erosion, and upward fining trend from red beds, trough evaporates to marine carbonates, with backstepping pattern of component sequences. These are though to be part of second order Upper Permian-Scythian rift-related sequence.

Val Gardena sandstone and the Bellerophon Formation ( Upper Permian ) in the Dolomites and Carnia show an overall transgressive trend and record the transition from continental red-bed to marine sedimentation in an extensional tectonic setting. The eastward progression of the Bellephron transgression resulted in the diachrony of the boundary between Val Gardena Sandstone and Bellephron Formation. The transgression was actually punctuated by a series of cyclical pulsations, which resulted in complex interfingering of terrigenous, evaporitic and carbonate deposits and in the subdivisions of the sedimentary succession into a number of sequences. The various vacies are essentially contempareous and follow one another along a paleoslope gently inclined towards the east, so that the red beds grade basinwards (i.e. eastwards ) through sabkha and lagoonal deposits into marine carbonates.

In the area between the Adige Valley and the Karawanken Mountains the Bellephron Formation ranges in thickness from 0 ( westernmost area ) to 360 m. 

The Bellephron Formation consists of a very complex array of lithofacies, its depositional area may be subdivided from west to east into
1) Coastal belt characterized by sabkha-type sediments interfingering with terminal fan deposits.
2) Hypersaline lagoon or restricted inner shelf, characterized by evaporates and carbonate deposits.
3) An inner carbonate shelf.
The transition from coastal to offshore environments was extremely gradual, suggesting a very gentle depositional gradient, and resulting in sedimentation particularly sensitive to environmental changes. The Bellephron Formation is sharply or transitional overlain by a regional widespread member between different sections, in the absence of outcrop continuity.

 The Upper Permian succession of the Southern Alps displays the typical features of early rift successions. The overall pattern is that of transgressive, backstepping and onlapping arrangements of deposits suggesting a background of regional subsidence. 

Sedimentation started in graben-like depressions, and was initially fed by local sources. Later as a result of regional subsidence and morphogenetic evolution of the basin, the original depositional areas joined, ultimately resulting in an unified and increasingly expanded depression with sedimentary fill progressively onlapping the margins of the basin. Basin opening is recorded by coarse scree and alluvial fan deposits. 

The thickness of Val Gardena Sandstone in the study area ranges from zero ( Trento area ) to more than 500 m ( Comelico area ). In the Dolomites and Carnia, the red beds grade into the evaporitic and carbonate deposits of the Bellerophon Formation. The transgression progressively encroached on western areas. A structural high between the Adige Valley and the Giudicarie Line prevented the westward progression of the transgression, so that the Bellerophron Formation appears on a broad scale as a sedimentary wedge pinching out westwards. The Bellephron Formation is overlain by the Lombardian Unit ( continental sediment ).

Terminal fan facies 
Generally single-storey ribbons and sheet like composite channelized bodies, generally of mixed load type, showing on average an upward increasing reduction in thickness and river bedload content; these are encased in an increasingly overbank of sediments, leading to low channel interconnections. This evolution is typically absent or very poorly developed in the marginal parts of the basin and in the less subsiding areas characterized by reduced thickness of sedimentary succession. Simple single-storey ribbons range from 0.9 to 4.3 m in thickness. The sediments involved range coarse sands, locally bearing granules and small pebbles, to fine sands and mudstone. Channel fills exhibit a sharp, fairly incised, irregular erosional base, sometimes with a remarkedly stepped appearance, floored by mudstone clasts and sometimes-reworked calcrete nodules. Vertically accreted ribbons commonly display a crudely developed fining-upward textural sequence, with trough cross bedding of upward decreasing scale, locally accompanied by planar lamination; small ribbons of this type may have been deposited by single flood events. Other ribbons show an inclined heterolithic stratification suggesting limited lateral migration, with muddy members of the couplets usually reaching the base of the channel.
Thick muddy intercalations, sometimes pedogenically modified, may occur in the lateral accretionary units indicating that the fill was highly episodic in some channels. Burrow networks are relatively common in the upper part of the channel fills.
Internal scouring surfaces, in place floored by mudstone clasts, are quite common, and several stages of scour and fill are characteristic, especially in channelized bodies of the inner more proximal zone of the system, and suggests highly fluctuating hydrodynamic conditions.
Sheet like sandstones, mostsly resulting from lateral and to a limited extend also vertical amalgation of ribbons and small-storey internal organization can be found.
Channel fills are interbedded with a great variety of interchannel sand and silt units deposited during flooding. Splay sandstones and commonly form a volumetrical large proportion of the total sand framework, especially near the transition into inferred sabkha sediments and may extend far into the interchannel areas, reflecting the extremely flashy and ephemeral nature of the associated streams. Splay deposits include both sheet sand layers showing virtual non-erosional basal contacts with the underlying sediments, and more discontinous and lenticular beds with broadly erosional bases. Sheet sandstone layers partly appear to be wings tapering away from channel sandstone bodies and sometimes coalescing to form extensive sheet-splays. The may be rich in vegetal debris and show small-scale flood sequences. Wave ripples draped by mud laminae are also locally observed.
The upper surface of some play sandstone layers show evidence of a local shallow scouring. Splay sandstones and associated mudstones in places show root traces and or invertebrate burrows and are occasionally interbedded with dolomite and gypsum layers. Horizons with mud cracks in the mudstones.
Spaly sandstones may appear organized into thickening and coarsening-upward sequences 6-10 m thick, displaying a clear upward increase in the sand/mud ratio. These consists of basal mudstone intervals with sparse, thin, sandstone interbeds passing up into thicker-bedded sheet-sandstones and eventually single channel fills.

Mouth bar 
Small-scale upward thickening and coarsening sequences 3-6 m thick are generally observed at the transition from lagoonal/marine to continental facies associations. Muddy layers alternate with thin-bedded sandstones in the lower part, and progressively disseappear, to grade upwards into a amalgated package of sandstone layers generally displaying unidirectional structures such as ripple-drift cross-lamination, trough cross bedding and planar-lamination; the sequence may be capped by erosive based channel sandstones. The facies association is thought to represents small mouth-bars encroaching on a shallow-water basin.

The transgression was actually punctuated by a series of cyclical pulsations, which resulted in complex interfingering of terrigenous, evaporitic and carbonate deposits and in the subdivisions of the sedimentary succession into a number of sequences. In the area between the Adige Valley and the Karawanken Mountains the Bellephron Formation ranges in thickness from 0 ( westernmost area ) to 360 m. 

The Bellephron Formation consists of a very complex array of lithofacies, its depositional area may be subdivided from west to east into
1) Coastal belt characterized by sabkha-type sediments interfingering with terminal fan deposits.
2) Hypersaline lagoon or restricted inner shelf, characterized by evaporates and carbonate deposits.
3) An inner carbonate shelf.
The transition from coastal to offshore environments was extremely gradual, suggesting a very gentle depositional gradient, and resulting in sedimentation particularly sensitive to environmental changes. The Bellephron Formation is sharply or transitional overlain by a regional widespread member between different sections, in the absence of outcrop continuity.

 The Upper Permian succession of the Southern Alps displays the typical features of early rift successions. The overall pattern is that of transgressive, backstepping and onlapping arrangements of deposits suggesting a background of regional subsidence. 

Sedimentation started in graben-like depressions, and was initially fed by local sources. Later as a result of regional subsidence and morphogenetic evolution of the basin, the original depositional areas joined, ultimately resulting in an unified and increasingly expanded depression with sedimentary fill progressively onlapping the margins of the basin. Basin opening is recorded by coarse scree and alluvial fan deposits.

Terminal fan facies 
Generally single-storey ribbons and sheet like composite channelized bodies, generally of mixed load type, showing on average an upward increasing reduction in thickness and river bedload content; these are encased in an increasingly overbank of sediments, leading to low channel interconnections. This evolution is typically absent or very poorly developed in the marginal parts of the basin and in the less subsiding areas characterized by reduced thickness of sedimentary succession. Simple single-storey ribbons range from 0.9 to 4.3 m in thickness. The sediments involved range coarse sands, locally bearing granules and small pebbles, to fine sands and mudstone. Channel fills exhibit a sharp, fairly incised, irregular erosional base, sometimes with a remarkedly stepped appearance, floored by mudstone clasts and sometimes-reworked calcrete nodules. Vertically accreted ribbons commonly display a crudely developed fining-upward textural sequence, with trough cross bedding of upward decreasing scale, locally accompanied by planar lamination; small ribbons of this type may have been deposited by single flood events. Other ribbons show an inclined heterolithic stratification suggesting limited lateral migration, with muddy members of the couplets usually reaching the base of the channel.
Thick muddy intercalations, sometimes pedogenically modified, may occur in the lateral accretionary units indicating that the fill was highly episodic in some channels. Burrow networks are relatively common in the upper part of the channel fills.
Internal scouring surfaces, in place floored by mudstone clasts, are quite common, and several stages of scour and fill are characteristic, especially in channelized bodies of the inner more proximal zone of the system, and suggests highly fluctuating hydrodynamic conditions.
Sheet like sandstones, mostsly resulting from lateral and to a limited extend also vertical amalgation of ribbons and small-storey internal organization can be found.
Channel fills are interbedded with a great variety of interchannel sand and silt units deposited during flooding. Splay sandstones and commonly form a volumetrical large proportion of the total sand framework, especially near the transition into inferred sabkha sediments and may extend far into the interchannel areas, reflecting the extremely flashy and ephemeral nature of the associated streams. Splay deposits include both sheet sand layers showing virtual non-erosional basal contacts with the underlying sediments, and more discontinous and lenticular beds with broadly erosional bases. Sheet sandstone layers partly appear to be wings tapering away from channel sandstone bodies and sometimes coalescing to form extensive sheet-splays. The may be rich in vegetal debris and show small-scale flood sequences. Wave ripples draped by mud laminae are also locally observed.
The upper surface of some play sandstone layers show evidence of a local shallow scouring. Splay sandstones and associated mudstones in places show root traces and or invertebrate burrows and are occasionally interbedded with dolomite and gypsum layers. Horizons with mud cracks in the mudstones.
Spaly sandstones may appear organized into thickening and coarsening-upward sequences 6-10 m thick, displaying a clear upward increase in the sand/mud ratio. These consists of basal mudstone intervals with sparse, thin, sandstone interbeds passing up into thicker-bedded sheet-sandstones and eventually single channel fills.

Mouth bar 
Small-scale upward thickening and coarsening sequences 3-6 m thick are generally observed at the transition from lagoonal/marine to continental facies associations. Muddy layers alternate with thin-bedded sandstones in the lower part, and progressively disseappear, to grade upwards into a amalgated package of sandstone layers generally displaying unidirectional structures such as ripple-drift cross-lamination, trough cross bedding and planar-lamination; the sequence may be capped by erosive based channel sandstones. The facies association is thought to represents small mouth-bars encroaching on a shallow-water basin.
geology_comments:
Rivers probably underwent a definite decrease in depth downstream and a sharp fall-off in their average discharge in the lower part of their courses, due to a number of factors including:
A) Loss of water by evapo-transpiration and lower precipitation.
B) Infiltration into a permeable alluvium.
The rivers were probably exotic, and reduced to a network of low-gradient, shallow, ephemeral wadi distributaries plugged during repetive flash-flooding events and subject to frequent avulsions.
