stratcomments: Marambio Group sediments of Humps Island (Santa Marta and López de Bertodano formations)
lithdescript: Massive sandstones (Facies A of Pirrie & Riding 1988) are generally confined to the lower 50 m of the section and a 20 m interval towards the top. The remainder\r\nof the section is predominantly mudstone (Facies C of Pirrie & Riding 1988). The boundary between the Herbert Sound Member and the Cape Lamb Member is seen at the top of the lower portion of mixed sandstone and mudstone, c. 35 m above the base of the section described by Pirrie & Riding (1988). The same lithological change exists 35-50 m above the base of the present section.
primary_reference: P. J. D. Dolding. 1992. Palynology of the Marambio Group (Upper Cretaceous) of northern Humps Island. Antartic Science 4(3):311-326
lithdescript.1: Massive sandstones (Facies A of Pirrie & Riding 1988) are generally confined to the lower 50 m of the section and a 20 m interval towards the top. The remainder\r\nof the section is predominantly mudstone (Facies C of Pirrie & Riding 1988). The boundary between the Herbert Sound Member and the Cape Lamb Member is seen at the top of the lower portion of mixed sandstone and mudstone, c. 35 m above the base of the section described by Pirrie & Riding (1988). The same lithological change exists 35-50 m above the base of the present section.
geology_comments:
Three distinct palaeoenvironrnents are invoked, based upon the relative abundance of certain commonly occurring taxa and significant changes in the composition of the palynomorph assemblages.

Interval 1 (DJ.288.1-7) appears to represent nearshore conditions, the high  proportion of spores and pollen (22-36% of total palynomorphs) supporting this suggestion.

Interval 2 (DJ.288.9-13) represents shallow palaeoenvironments. The acanthomorph acritarch Michrystridium spp. increases to a peak abundance (26% of total palynomorphs) in sample DJ.288.11. This genus is indicative of relatively shallow conditions close to a palaeocoastline (Wall 1965). In the same sample, the proportions of Phelodinium exilicornutum and Senoniasphuera spp. (10% and 17% of total palynomorphs respectively) also increase to their maximum abundance.

Interval 3 (DJ.288.14 & 15) represents a change to a more distal palaeoenvironment.

lithdescript: Section of tuffaceous sandstones, siltstones and mudstones that extends up to 10 m laterally and is approximately 6 m thick, of which about 4 m is fossiliferous. The upper conglomerate has an erosive junction with the fossiliferous section. The beds dip 15°S and display contorted lamination in three or probably four upwardcoarsening cycles, each beginning with very thin beds or lenses of bright coal and tuffaceous mudstones (Dutra et al., 1996). At the top there is a conglomerate that consists of chaotically dispersed volcaniclastic and tuffaceous blocks up to 50 cm in diameter, and pieces of wood and coal.

lithdescript.1: A Formação Codó compreende uma seqüência de folhelhos. calcários e evaporitos intercalados.
geology_comments: Vários fósseis marinhos tem sido referidos, conforme pode ser visto na figura 2, para a Formação Codó. A própria seqüência sedimentar parece confirmar a influência marinha na deposição da unidade. Nas associações ora estudadas, contudo, elementos do microplâncton marinho parecem totalmente ausentes,\r\ncom exceção de formas retrabalhadas do Devoniano. Evidentemente esta observação não objetiva negar categoricamente a existência de tal influência, já que os resultados apresentados são praticamente pontuais, não representando portanto,\r\numa conclusão válida para toda a extensão da bacia.

lithdescript: It has characterized the Cerro Negro Formation in five pyroclastic units widely distributed in the area, two main groups of lavas and intrusive, and sedimentary terms, that including conglomerates, shales and sandstones. \r\nSedimentary description: At the bottom is siliceous volcaniclastic rocks, followed by welded ignimbrites, then tuffs lapilli mainly basaltic and upper  sandstones and basaltic conglomerates.
primary_reference: E. I. Vera. 2010. Estudios anatómicos en paleofloras del Aptiano de Antártida y Patagonia, y su comparación. Universidad de Buenos Aires. Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales
lithdescript.1: It has characterized the Cerro Negro Formation in five pyroclastic units widely distributed in the area, two main groups of lavas and intrusive, and sedimentary terms, that including conglomerates, shales and sandstones. \r\nSedimentary description: At the bottom is siliceous volcaniclastic rocks, followed by welded ignimbrites, then tuffs lapilli mainly basaltic and upper  sandstones and basaltic conglomerates.
geology_comments: An environment influenced by volcanic activity, with initial volcaniclastic contribution proportionally greater than the rate of subsidence, so that is not recognized intereruptivos deposit development. Subsequently, the increase in subsidence rate and a decrease in volcanic activity would have allowed the establishment of a lake, whose deposition would end with another period of volcanic activity. The last stage of deposition of the unit shows the development of fluvial environments with paleosol development.

geology_comments: The paleoenvironmental interpretation derived from the deposits of the unit suggests the existence of traccional or suspensive flows, related to channeled flows broad and shallow valleys,generated by rainfall.Furthermore, it would have created bodies of water muddy to sandy and incipient paleosols,the latter due to subaerial exposure. At the same time, the existence of tuffaceous deposits  suggest the existence of intermittent volcanic activity.

lithdescript: Cladera 2002. This unit consists of siliciclastic and volcaniclastic facies, and is named for the locality Anfiteatro de Ticó, a wide arc containing numerous fossil outcrops, located northwest of Estancia La Magdalena.\r\n\r\nNote: La unidad se compone de litoacies silicoclásticas y volcaniclásticas. Entre las primeras, con tonos castaños, se incluyen ocnglomerados clasto soporte macizos (Gm) y con estructuras cruzadas en artesa (Gt), areniscas gruesas hasta sabulíticas con estructuras cruzadas en artesa (St) y escasas areniscas finas con óndulas asimétricas de corriente (Sr). Asimismo, aparecen arcillitas y imolitas gris oscuro, con estructuras macizas o con discretas estructuras lentiforms arenosas (linsen) (Fm), laminación (Fsc) y mostrando escasas y pequeñas raíces axiales con ramificaciones (Fr). Su composición es caolinítica. (Cladera, 2002)

geogcomments: The fossil remains were recovered from unnamed beds at the Puesto Baibián locality, Central-North Chubut Province, Patagonia.
stratcomments:
-The fossil remains were recovered from unnamed beds at the Puesto Baibián   locality.
-For the purposes of this article, we can say that the Baibián Beds are  definitely post-Paleocene in age and that they preceded the deposition of the  Late Oligocene–Early Miocene Sarmiento Group in the same area.

-These beds, which we informally name here in as the Baibián Beds, overlie the  Late Cretaceous La Colonia Formation and are overlain by altered basaltic lavas of  unknown age, which in turn are overimposed by the tuffaceous Sarmiento Group.
primary_reference: M. A. Gandolfo, M. Zamaloa, and N. R. Cúneo, A. Archangelsky. 2009. Potamogetonaceae Fossil Fruits from the Tertiary of Patagonia, Argentina. International Journal of Plant Sciences 170(3):419-428
time_overlap: Danian, Selandian, Thanetian, Ypresian, Lutetian, Bartonian, Priabonian, Rupelian, Chattian
geology_comments: The Baibián Beds are around 18 m thick and are composed mainly of a lower  interval of fluvial/alluvial conglomerates, which suggest a post-Cretaceous  reactivation surface, followed by finely laminated fine-grained lacustrine  deposits. The latter bear a rich freshwater aquatic biota, including  the potamogetonaceous remains described in this article, Equisetum, frogs,  turtles, fishes, and a well-preserved microflora with a high abundance of freshwater algal components that mostly records the local plant community.
collection_comments: Fossils are housed at the Paleobotanical Collection of the Museo Paleontológico  Egidio Feruglio, Chubut, Argentina (MPEF Pb 2010–2013, 2408, and 2409, MPEF Palin).

geogcomments: Formación del Buey, sierra de Famatina, provincia de La Rioja.
lithdescript: La asociación palinológica proviene de un único horizonte fértil (Muestra FDB1), ubicado próximo a la base de la Formación del Buey. Corresponde a un nivel de pelitas verdes a amarillentas que representa a la facies interpretada como depósitos lacustres someros.\r\n\r\nLa Formación del Buey es una unidad predominantemente pelítica, de color rosado pardusca a rojiza. Ocasionalmente, se intercalan conglomerados finos mantiformes y lenticulares, y niveles carbonáticos tabulares, en parte nodulares y en parte finamente laminados con extensión lateral (mayor a 1km).
primary_reference: V. D. Barreda, E. G. Ottone, and F. M. Dávila, R. A. Astini. 2006. Edad y paleoambiente de la Formación del Buey (Mioceno), sierra de Famatina, La Rioja, Argentina: evidencias sedimentológicas y palinológicas. Ameghiniana 42(1):215-226

geology_comments: El horizonte fértil de que se colectaron los fósiles es interpretado como depósitos lacustres someros. La depositación de la Formación del Buey habría estado controlada por una sedimentación mayormente fluvial, en un período de relativa estabilidad del paisaje, con desarrollo de cuerpos lacustres semiperennes.

collection_name: Sample 3-1, LC-II pit, Lost Chicken site
geogcomments: Upper pit, above the highway.
stratcomments: Sample from peat just below unit F. Lost Chicken tephra dated at 2.6 +/- 0.45 Ma based on zircon fission-track. Unit C sediments just below LCT at Section 91-2 have a normal remanent magnetic polarity (Fig. 3), which suggests that LCT was deposited during the youngest normal subchron of the Gauss chron, that is, between 2.581 and 3.040 myr (Cande and Kent, 1995). The reversed magnetic polarity of Unit A likely means that it was deposited during the Kaena subchron (3.040–3.110 myr; Cande and Kent, 1995), whereas the reversed magnetic polarity of Units D and E, which occur above LCT, suggests that these silty sediments accumulated during the early part of the Matuyama chron.
primary_reference: J. V. Matthews, J. A. Westgate, and L. Ovenden, L. D. Carter, T. Fouch. 2003. Stratigraphy, fossils, and age of sediments at the upper pit of the Lost Chicken gold mine: new information on the late Pliocene environment of east central Alaska. Quaternary Research 60:9-18

geogcomments: The fossiliferous sediment outcrops in a cutting situated on an abandoned logging road approximately 2 km south of the Little Rapid River.\r\nRoad cutting in the northwest of Tasmania, 35 km south of Smithton. The sediments are located in an old river valley at relatively low altitude (90 m above sea level), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
stratcomments: The fossil-bearing mudstone has been dated by palynological correlation by M. K. Macphail. He considers that the mudstone belongs to the lower Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone of Stover & Partridge, 1973 (hill & Bigwood, 1987).  \r\nThe mudstone lens has been dated as Late Oligocene based on pollen analysis (Hill, 1987).\r\nThe sediments are dated palynologically as Early Oligocene (Macphail et al. 1994), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
lithdescript: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The upper sandy unit (approximately 50 cm thick) becomes lighter in colour higher up in the cutting, and eventually gives way to several metres of very pale-coloured sand with only fine particulate organic matter scattered through it. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1991 were extracted from mudstone lens.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill, G. J. Jordan, and R. J. Carpenter. 1993. Taxodiaceous Macrofossils from Tertiary and Quaternary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 6(3):237-249
lithdescript.1: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The upper sandy unit (approximately 50 cm thick) becomes lighter in colour higher up in the cutting, and eventually gives way to several metres of very pale-coloured sand with only fine particulate organic matter scattered through it. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1991 were extracted from mudstone lens.
geology_comments: It is likely that the Little Rapid River deposit represents a Tertiary lake which has undergone a dramatic change in depositional regimes. The lower unit is characteristic of a low energy environment such as the centre of a lake with low stream input. Organic laminations would be the result of fluctuating stream flow (possibly seasonal), the plant matter most probably being derived from vegetation lining inflowing creeks and streams or from the lake edge itself.
collection_comments: Fossils collected by R. S. Hill from 1992 to 1998 (Guerin & Hill, 2003).

geogcomments: The Pioneer tin mine is approximately 1 km north of the township of Pioneer in the Ringarooma Valley.
stratcomments: The most recent treatment of the age of the sediments has been made by Macphail et al. (1994) who consider them to be Late Oligocene-Early Miocene based on palynological correlation.\r\n- Overall, the data strongly indicate an Oligocene age for the flora, and possibly Early Oligocene (Wells & Hill, 1989).\r\n
lithdescript: According to Morrison (1980) the stratigraphy can be considered in terms of two sequences: 1) a lower sequence, up to 6 m thick, of cross-bedded and near horizontally stratified gravels, large scale trough cross-bedded granules with  very coarse sands and minor gravels, planar cross-bedded sands, and units rich in organic matter with associated sandy clay; and 2) an upper sequence extending to the present soil, with possible modification in the top 2 to 5 m, consisting essentially of trough cross-bedded quartz granules and coarse sands, lenses and sheets of white clay, and clayey, organic-rich units.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill, G. J. Jordan, and R. J. Carpenter. 1993. Taxodiaceous Macrofossils from Tertiary and Quaternary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 6(3):237-249
lithdescript.1: According to Morrison (1980) the stratigraphy can be considered in terms of two sequences: 1) a lower sequence, up to 6 m thick, of cross-bedded and near horizontally stratified gravels, large scale trough cross-bedded granules with  very coarse sands and minor gravels, planar cross-bedded sands, and units rich in organic matter with associated sandy clay; and 2) an upper sequence extending to the present soil, with possible modification in the top 2 to 5 m, consisting essentially of trough cross-bedded quartz granules and coarse sands, lenses and sheets of white clay, and clayey, organic-rich units.
geology_comments: Pioneer sediments represent a braided fluvial fan which originated from steep slopes to the east and south-east. The fossil-bearing lenses therefore represent areas which were cut off from the main flow resulting in bodies of still water from which fine sediments and plant debris settled. The braided fluvial fan represents a high energy environment and it is likely that each fossil-bearing lens represents a short term event.
taxonomy_comments: 197 imbricate podocarp specimens (Wells & Hill, 1989).

geogcomments: The site occurs in a road cutting only a few metres above sea level at Regatta Point, Macquarie Harbour.
stratcomments: The Regatta Point fossils are contained within transported blocks of sediment which have been dated by palynological correlation as Early or possibly Middle Pleistocene (Macphail et al. 1993). Dated as Late Pliocene-Early Pleistocene by Hill and Macphail, 1985; Wells & Hill, 1989.
lithdescript: The fossil occur in soft mudstone blocks situated in a glacifluvial outwash gravel above an Early Eocene mudstone. \r\nThe mudstone blocks are composed of quartz grains, black organic fragments,\r\nwhole plant structures and cream-coloured mud flakes all dispersed through a dark brown-grey mudstone matrix (Wells & Hill, 1989). Macrofossils from Jordan, 1997 were extracted from mudstone, siltstone and sandstone clasts within the gravels.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill, G. J. Jordan, and R. J. Carpenter. 1993. Taxodiaceous Macrofossils from Tertiary and Quaternary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 6(3):237-249
lithdescript.1: The fossil occur in soft mudstone blocks situated in a glacifluvial outwash gravel above an Early Eocene mudstone. \r\nThe mudstone blocks are composed of quartz grains, black organic fragments,\r\nwhole plant structures and cream-coloured mud flakes all dispersed through a dark brown-grey mudstone matrix (Wells & Hill, 1989). Macrofossils from Jordan, 1997 were extracted from mudstone, siltstone and sandstone clasts within the gravels.
geology_comments: The blocks have been transported an unkwown distance from the original site of deposition. It is unlikely that they have travelled far, since they are large (1 m3), close together and very angular, with little sign of erosion.\r\n\r\nThe fine-grained nature of the sediment matrix indicates distal deposition in a low-energy environment such as a lake, river estuary or a shallow inland harbour such as the one existing there today (Wells & Hill, 1989).
collection_comments: Repository: Department of Plant Science at the University of Tasmania.\r\npollen count min. 400 identifiable pollen and spores (Jordan et al., 1995).
taxonomy_comments: Includes macrofossils and microfossils.

geogcomments: Quarry exposure, North Maslin Sands, Maslin Bay, South Australia.\r\nSite is located ca. 35 km south of Adelaide, South Australia (Carpenter et al., 2006).

lithdescript: Clay lens, lens of carbonaceous mudstone and siltstone in a quarry exposure of the North Maslin Sands (Reynolds, 1953).
primary_reference: D. T. Blackburn. 1981. Tertiary megafossil flora of Maslin Bay, South Australia: numerical taxonomic study of selected leaves. Alcheringa 5(1):9-28
lithdescript.1: Clay lens, lens of carbonaceous mudstone and siltstone in a quarry exposure of the North Maslin Sands (Reynolds, 1953).
geology_comments: The fossils were recovered from clay lenses in the nonmarine, deltaic North Maslin Sand, which formed in quiet water after meandering fluvial channels were cut off to form oxbow lakes (Carpenter et al., 2006).

geogcomments: The Pioneer tin mine is approximately 1 km north of the township of Pioneer in the Ringarooma Valley.
stratcomments: The most recent treatment of the age of the sediments has been made by Macphail et al. (1994) who consider them to be Late Oligocene-Early Miocene based on palynological correlation.\r\n- Overall, the data strongly indicate an Oligocene age for the flora, and possibly Early Oligocene (Wells & Hill, 1989).\r\n
lithdescript: According to Morrison (1980) the stratigraphy can be considered in terms of two sequences: 1) a lower sequence, up to 6 m thick, of cross-bedded and near horizontally stratified gravels, large scale trough cross-bedded granules with  very coarse sands and minor gravels, planar cross-bedded sands, and units rich in organic matter with associated sandy clay; and 2) an upper sequence extending to the present soil, with possible modification in the top 2 to 5 m, consisting essentially of trough cross-bedded quartz granules and coarse sands, lenses and sheets of white clay, and clayey, organic-rich units.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill and M. K. Macphail. 1983. Reconstruction of the Oligocene vegetation at Pioneer, northeast Tasmania. Alcheringa 7:281-299
lithdescript.1: According to Morrison (1980) the stratigraphy can be considered in terms of two sequences: 1) a lower sequence, up to 6 m thick, of cross-bedded and near horizontally stratified gravels, large scale trough cross-bedded granules with  very coarse sands and minor gravels, planar cross-bedded sands, and units rich in organic matter with associated sandy clay; and 2) an upper sequence extending to the present soil, with possible modification in the top 2 to 5 m, consisting essentially of trough cross-bedded quartz granules and coarse sands, lenses and sheets of white clay, and clayey, organic-rich units.
geology_comments: Pioneer sediments represent a braided fluvial fan which originated from steep slopes to the east and south-east. The fossil-bearing lenses therefore represent areas which were cut off from the main flow resulting in bodies of still water from which fine sediments and plant debris settled. The braided fluvial fan represents a high energy environment and it is likely that each fossil-bearing lens represents a short term event.
taxonomy_comments: 197 imbricate podocarp specimens (Wells & Hill, 1989).

collection_name: ALCOA Anglesea Site II coal mine
geogcomments: 2 km north-east of Anglesea. Clay lens of the new Block Two Site, c. 0.5 km from the lenses of the original mine, Christophel (1984).
stratcomments: The deposit is considered to be Upper Eocene (Christophel 1981) and recent palynological investigations (A. Partridge, Esso (Australia), personal communication) support this, placing two vertically distinct lenses both in the Middle Nothofagadites asperus Zone (Christophel, 1984).\r\nThese sediments represent the Anglesea member of the Demon Bluff Formation\r\n(Abele et al. 1976) and, in a personal communication quoted by Christophel (1984), Partridge placed the lenses in the upper subzonule of Stover and Partridge's (1973) lower Nothofagidities aspersus Zone, middle to late Eocene (Greenwood, 1987).
lithdescript: clay lens of the new Block Two Site, c. 0.5 km from the lenses of the original mine. Two laterally extensive fossiliferous lenses in the mudstones and unconsolidated sands unconformably overlying the brown coal of the Eastern View Formation occurs c. 70 m below the ground surface and extends c. 60 m laterally along the south-east face of the Block Two Site. The lens varies in thickness from 0.5 to 3.0 m.
primary_reference: D. R. Greenwood. 1987. Early Tertiary Podocarpaceae: Megafossils from the Eocene Anglesea Locality, Victoria, Australia. Australian Journal of Botany 35(2):111-133
lithdescript.1: clay lens of the new Block Two Site, c. 0.5 km from the lenses of the original mine. geology_comments: Fine mudstone and clay rich in mummified leaves and probably represent deposition in cut-off branches of a meandering river system.

geogcomments: The site occurs in a road cutting only a few metres above sea level at Regatta Point, Macquarie Harbour.
stratcomments: The Regatta Point fossils are contained within transported blocks of sediment which have been dated by palynological correlation as Early or possibly Middle Pleistocene (Macphail et al. 1993). Dated as Late Pliocene-Early Pleistocene by Hill and Macphail, 1985; Wells & Hill, 1989.
lithdescript: The fossil occur in soft mudstone blocks situated in a glacifluvial outwash gravel above an Early Eocene mudstone. \r\nThe mudstone blocks are composed of quartz grains, black organic fragments,\r\nwhole plant structures and cream-coloured mud flakes all dispersed through a dark brown-grey mudstone matrix (Wells & Hill, 1989). Macrofossils from Jordan, 1997 were extracted from mudstone, siltstone and sandstone clasts within the gravels.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill and M. K. Macphail. 1985. A fossil flora from rafted Plio Pleistocene mudstones at Regatta Point, Tasmania. Australian Journal of Botany 33:497-517
lithdescript.1: The fossil occur in soft mudstone blocks situated in a glacifluvial outwash gravel above an Early Eocene mudstone. \r\nThe mudstone blocks are composed of quartz grains, black organic fragments,\r\nwhole plant structures and cream-coloured mud flakes all dispersed through a dark brown-grey mudstone matrix (Wells & Hill, 1989). Macrofossils from Jordan, 1997 were extracted from mudstone, siltstone and sandstone clasts within the gravels.
geology_comments: The blocks have been transported an unkwown distance from the original site of deposition. It is unlikely that they have travelled far, since they are large (1 m3), close together and very angular, with little sign of erosion.\r\n\r\nThe fine-grained nature of the sediment matrix indicates distal deposition in a low-energy environment such as a lake, river estuary or a shallow inland harbour such as the one existing there today (Wells & Hill, 1989).
collection_comments: Repository: Department of Plant Science at the University of Tasmania.\r\npollen count min. 400 identifiable pollen and spores (Jordan et al., 1995).
taxonomy_comments: Includes macrofossils and microfossils.

geogcomments: The fossiliferous sediment outcrops in a cutting situated on an abandoned logging road approximately 2 km south of the Little Rapid River.\r\nRoad cutting in the northwest of Tasmania, 35 km south of Smithton. The sediments are located in an old river valley at relatively low altitude (90 m above sea level), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
stratcomments: The fossil-bearing mudstone has been dated by palynological correlation by M. K. Macphail. He considers that the mudstone belongs to the lower Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone of Stover & Partridge, 1973 (hill & Bigwood, 1987). Macphail (in Hill 1987) suggested a Late Oligocene age for the flora.\r\nThe sediments are dated palynologically as Early Oligocene (Macphail et al. 1994) in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
lithdescript: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The lower unit is at least 2 m in depth and is composed of a very fine-grained dark grey mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils. mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils.\r\nAbove the organic layer which separates the two units the sediment changes suddenly to a coarser grained material composed of dark grey sands, once again rich in black organic material. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1989 & Hill and Carpenter, 1989 were recovered from the fluviatile sands of this place.
primary_reference: P. M. Wells and R. S. Hill. 1989. Fossil Imbricate-leaved Podocarpaceae from Tertiary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 2(4):387-423
lithdescript.1: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The lower unit is at least 2 m in depth and is composed of a very fine-grained dark grey mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils. mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils.\r\nAbove the organic layer which separates the two units the sediment changes suddenly to a coarser grained material composed of dark grey sands, once again rich in black organic material. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1989 & Hill and Carpenter, 1989 were recovered from the fluviatile sands of this place.
geology_comments: It is likely that the Little Rapid River deposit represents a Tertiary lake which has undergone a dramatic change in depositional regimes. The lower unit is characteristic of a low energy environment such as the centre of a lake with low stream input. Organic laminations would be the result of fluctuating stream flow (possibly seasonal), the plant matter most probably being derived from vegetation lining inflowing creeks and streams or from the lake edge itself.
collection_comments: Fossils collected by R. S. Hill from 1992 to 1998 (Guerin & Hill, 2003).

geogcomments: The Monpeelyata deposit is exposed in a canal cut by the Hydro-Electric Commission to connect the two impoundments of Little Pine Lagoon and Lake Echo.
stratcomments: The sediments are regarded as probably late Oligocene or early Miocene age based on analysis of microflora and radiometric dates of closely associated basalts (Hill & Gibson, 1986).\r\nThe area has been dated using K-Ar analysis, the age range 23.6-21.8 Myr (Sutherland et al. 1973).These results agree with the palynological data, and an earliest Miocene age is therefore proposed for the Monpeelyata deposit, with the probable age falling within the period 21.8-23.6 Myr (M.K. Macphail, personal communication).\r\nThe age of Monpeelyata is based on a combination of palynological data and K-Ar dates on basalt flows in the area surrounding Great Lake. Both sets of data point to the Monpeelyata flora being no younger than earliest Miocene. The maximum age is less well defined although the absence of a large number of species found in Oligocene palynoflora in northern Tasmania (Hill & Macphail, 1983; Hill, 1987) suggests that the flora is unlikely to be older than the (latest?) Late Oligocene. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
lithdescript: The fossils occur in a mudstone lens approximately 15 m long and about 1.5 m thick which has been exposed in a channel-cutting on the Central Plateau. The lens is overlain by about 2 m of basalt. \r\nThe plant fossils described by Macphail and Hill 1991 come from a mudstone exposed in the west wall of the Monpeelyata Canal which diverts water from the Ouse River into the Lake Echo hydroelectic impoundment. The exposure occurs directly next to the bridge on the Monpeelyata Canal service road. The mudstone lens forms part of a thin (<2 m?) concave lenticular sedimentary sequence that overlies Jurassic dolerite and is overlain by massive to vesicular, alkali olivine basalt. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
primary_reference: P. M. Wells and R. S. Hill. 1989. Fossil Imbricate-leaved Podocarpaceae from Tertiary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 2(4):387-423

The lens is overlain by about 2 m of basalt. \r\nThe plant fossils described by Macphail and Hill 1991 come from a mudstone exposed in the west wall of the Monpeelyata Canal which diverts water from the Ouse River into the Lake Echo hydroelectic impoundment. The exposure occurs directly next to the bridge on the Monpeelyata Canal service road. The mudstone lens forms part of a thin (<2 m?) concave lenticular sedimentary sequence that overlies Jurassic dolerite and is overlain by massive to vesicular, alkali olivine basalt. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
geology_comments: It is probable that the depositional environment was a shallow freshwater lake or tarn similar to the many alpine lakes which currently occur in the Tasmanian highlands (Hill 1988).\r\nAbundant remains of the freshwater hydrophyte Isoetes (Hill, 1988) and the fine grain size of the emergent sedimentary rock indicate a low energy depositional environment, probably a shallow pond, a sluggish river channel, or less likely a shallow, sheltered lake bay, subaerially exposed before or during lava extrusions. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
taxonomy_comments: 830 podocarpaceous specimens.

geogcomments: The Monpeelyata deposit is exposed in a canal cut by the Hydro-Electric Commission to connect the two impoundments of Little Pine Lagoon and Lake Echo.
stratcomments: The sediments are regarded as probably late Oligocene or early Miocene age based on analysis of microflora and radiometric dates of closely associated basalts (Hill & Gibson, 1986).\r\nThe area has been dated using K-Ar analysis, the age range 23.6-21.8 Myr (Sutherland et al. 1973).These results agree with the palynological data, and an earliest Miocene age is therefore proposed for the Monpeelyata deposit, with the probable age falling within the period 21.8-23.6 Myr (M.K. Macphail, personal communication).\r\nThe age of Monpeelyata is based on a combination of palynological data and K-Ar dates on basalt flows in the area surrounding Great Lake. Both sets of data point to the Monpeelyata flora being no younger than earliest Miocene. The maximum age is less well defined although the absence of a large number of species found in Oligocene palynoflora in northern Tasmania (Hill & Macphail, 1983; Hill, 1987) suggests that the flora is unlikely to be older than the (latest?) Late Oligocene. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
lithdescript: The fossils occur in a mudstone lens approximately 15 m long and about 1.5 m thick which has been exposed in a channel-cutting on the Central Plateau. The lens is overlain by about 2 m of basalt. \r\nThe plant fossils described by Macphail and Hill 1991 come from a mudstone exposed in the west wall of the Monpeelyata Canal which diverts water from the Ouse River into the Lake Echo hydroelectic impoundment. The exposure occurs directly next to the bridge on the Monpeelyata Canal service road. The mudstone lens forms part of a thin (<2 m?) concave lenticular sedimentary sequence that overlies Jurassic dolerite and is overlain by massive to vesicular, alkali olivine basalt. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)

geogcomments: The fossiliferous sediment outcrops in a cutting situated on an abandoned logging road approximately 2 km south of the Little Rapid River.\r\nRoad cutting in the northwest of Tasmania, 35 km south of Smithton. The sediments are located in an old river valley at relatively low altitude (90 m above sea level), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
stratcomments: The fossil-bearing mudstone has been dated by palynological correlation by M. K. Macphail. He considers that the mudstone belongs to the lower Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone of Stover & Partridge, 1973 (hill & Bigwood, 1987).  \r\nThe mudstone lens has been dated as Late Oligocene based on pollen analysis (Hill, 1987).\r\nThe sediments are dated palynologically as Early Oligocene (Macphail et al. 1994), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
lithdescript: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The upper sandy unit (approximately 50 cm thick) becomes lighter in colour higher up in the cutting, and eventually gives way to several metres of very pale-coloured sand with only fine particulate organic matter scattered through it. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1991 were extracted from mudstone lens.
primary_reference: P. M. Wells and R. S. Hill. 1989. Fossil Imbricate-leaved Podocarpaceae from Tertiary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 2(4):387-423

geology_comments: It is likely that the Little Rapid River deposit represents a Tertiary lake which has undergone a dramatic change in depositional regimes. The lower unit is characteristic of a low energy environment such as the centre of a lake with low stream input. Organic laminations would be the result of fluctuating stream flow (possibly seasonal), the plant matter most probably being derived from vegetation lining inflowing creeks and streams or from the lake edge itself.
collection_comments: Fossils collected by R. S. Hill from 1992 to 1998 (Guerin & Hill, 2003).

geogcomments: The Pioneer tin mine is approximately 1 km north of the township of Pioneer in the Ringarooma Valley.
stratcomments: The most recent treatment of the age of the sediments has been made by Macphail et al. (1994) who consider them to be Late Oligocene-Early Miocene based on palynological correlation.\r\n- Overall, the data strongly indicate an Oligocene age for the flora, and possibly Early Oligocene (Wells & Hill, 1989).\r\n
lithdescript: According to Morrison (1980) the stratigraphy can be considered in terms of two sequences: 1) a lower sequence, up to 6 m thick, of cross-bedded and near horizontally stratified gravels, large scale trough cross-bedded granules with  very coarse sands and minor gravels, planar cross-bedded sands, and units rich in organic matter with associated sandy clay; and 2) an upper sequence extending to the present soil, with possible modification in the top 2 to 5 m, consisting essentially of trough cross-bedded quartz granules and coarse sands, lenses and sheets of white clay, and clayey, organic-rich units.
primary_reference: P. M. Wells and R. S. Hill. 1989. Fossil Imbricate-leaved Podocarpaceae from Tertiary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 2(4):387-423
lithdescript.1: According to Morrison (1980) the stratigraphy can be considered in terms of two sequences: 1) a lower sequence, up to 6 m thick, of cross-bedded and near horizontally stratified gravels, large scale trough cross-bedded granules with  very coarse sands and minor gravels, planar cross-bedded sands, and units rich in organic matter with associated sandy clay; and 2) an upper sequence extending to the present soil, with possible modification in the top 2 to 5 m, consisting essentially of trough cross-bedded quartz granules and coarse sands, lenses and sheets of white clay, and clayey, organic-rich units.
geology_comments: Pioneer sediments represent a braided fluvial fan which originated from steep slopes to the east and south-east. The fossil-bearing lenses therefore represent areas which were cut off from the main flow resulting in bodies of still water from which fine sediments and plant debris settled. The braided fluvial fan represents a high energy environment and it is likely that each fossil-bearing lens represents a short term event.
taxonomy_comments: 197 imbricate podocarp specimens (Wells & Hill, 1989).

geogcomments: The Monpeelyata deposit is exposed in a canal cut by the Hydro-Electric Commission to connect the two impoundments of Little Pine Lagoon and Lake Echo.
stratcomments: The sediments are regarded as probably late Oligocene or early Miocene age based on analysis of microflora and radiometric dates of closely associated basalts (Hill & Gibson, 1986).\r\nThe area has been dated using K-Ar analysis, the age range 23.6-21.8 Myr (Sutherland et al. 1973).These results agree with the palynological data, and an earliest Miocene age is therefore proposed for the Monpeelyata deposit, with the probable age falling within the period 21.8-23.6 Myr (M.K. Macphail, personal communication).\r\nThe age of Monpeelyata is based on a combination of palynological data and K-Ar dates on basalt flows in the area surrounding Great Lake. Both sets of data point to the Monpeelyata flora being no younger than earliest Miocene. The maximum age is less well defined although the absence of a large number of species found in Oligocene palynoflora in northern Tasmania (Hill & Macphail, 1983; Hill, 1987) suggests that the flora is unlikely to be older than the (latest?) Late Oligocene. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
lithdescript: The fossils occur in a mudstone lens approximately 15 m long and about 1.5 m thick which has been exposed in a channel-cutting on the Central Plateau. The lens is overlain by about 2 m of basalt. \r\nThe plant fossils described by Macphail and Hill 1991 come from a mudstone exposed in the west wall of the Monpeelyata Canal which diverts water from the Ouse River into the Lake Echo hydroelectic impoundment. The exposure occurs directly next to the bridge on the Monpeelyata Canal service road. The mudstone lens forms part of a thin (<2 m?) concave lenticular sedimentary sequence that overlies Jurassic dolerite and is overlain by massive to vesicular, alkali olivine basalt. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)

geogcomments: The Pioneer tin mine is approximately 1 km north of the township of Pioneer in the Ringarooma Valley.
stratcomments: The most recent treatment of the age of the sediments has been made by Macphail et al. (1994) who consider them to be Late Oligocene-Early Miocene based on palynological correlation.\r\n- Overall, the data strongly indicate an Oligocene age for the flora, and possibly Early Oligocene (Wells & Hill, 1989).\r\n
lithdescript: According to Morrison (1980) the stratigraphy can be considered in terms of two sequences: 1) a lower sequence, up to 6 m thick, of cross-bedded and near horizontally stratified gravels, large scale trough cross-bedded granules with  very coarse sands and minor gravels, planar cross-bedded sands, and units rich in organic matter with associated sandy clay; and 2) an upper sequence extending to the present soil, with possible modification in the top 2 to 5 m, consisting essentially of trough cross-bedded quartz granules and coarse sands, lenses and sheets of white clay, and clayey, organic-rich units.
primary_reference: P. M. Wells and R. S. Hill. 1989. Fossil Imbricate-leaved Podocarpaceae from Tertiary Sediments in Tasmania. Australian Systematic Botany 2(4):387-423

geology_comments: Pioneer sediments represent a braided fluvial fan which originated from steep slopes to the east and south-east. The fossil-bearing lenses therefore represent areas which were cut off from the main flow resulting in bodies of still water from which fine sediments and plant debris settled. The braided fluvial fan represents a high energy environment and it is likely that each fossil-bearing lens represents a short term event.

Further palynological assessment suggests that the flora is likely to be in the Late Eocene to Oligocene range based on the high proportion of Nothofagus brassii-type and Phyllocladidites mawsonii pollen (Carpenter & Hill, 1988).
The palynoflora has been assigned to the early Oligocene by Macphail et al. 1994. The presence of Cyatheacidites annulatus provides a confident Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone (Stover and Partridge 1973) maximum age, but the upper age limits are less certain owing to possible diachronism in the times of extinction of accessory species such as Beaupreadites verrucosus, Granodiporites nebulosus and Triporopollenites ambiguus. (Hill et al. 2008)
lithdescript: The deposit unconformably overlies folded quartzose arenaceous (Moina Sandstone) meta-sediments. The fossiliferous rock is a creamy-yellow to light brown-grey laminated siltstone with alternations of thin sand layers. Fossils from Hill & Carpenter, 1988 were recovered from mudstone of the same locality.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill and R. J. Carpenter. 1989. Tertiary gymnosperms from Tasmania: Cupressaceae. Alcheringa 13:89-102

geology_comments: The fine laminated siltstone with terrestrial plant fragments indicates a low energy depositional environment such as a lake centre. The sand layers may indicate fluctuating stream inflow on the lake edges.\r\nThe Cethana deposit had an Early Oligocene altitude of about 300 m. It formed at a time for which there is evidence of regional glacial activity (Macphail et al. 1993), in Carpenter & Jordan, 1997.

geogcomments: The Monpeelyata deposit is exposed in a canal cut by the Hydro-Electric Commission to connect the two impoundments of Little Pine Lagoon and Lake Echo.
stratcomments: The sediments are regarded as probably late Oligocene or early Miocene age based on analysis of microflora and radiometric dates of closely associated basalts (Hill & Gibson, 1986).\r\nThe area has been dated using K-Ar analysis, the age range 23.6-21.8 Myr (Sutherland et al. 1973).These results agree with the palynological data, and an earliest Miocene age is therefore proposed for the Monpeelyata deposit, with the probable age falling within the period 21.8-23.6 Myr (M.K. Macphail, personal communication).\r\nThe age of Monpeelyata is based on a combination of palynological data and K-Ar dates on basalt flows in the area surrounding Great Lake. Both sets of data point to the Monpeelyata flora being no younger than earliest Miocene. The maximum age is less well defined although the absence of a large number of species found in Oligocene palynoflora in northern Tasmania (Hill & Macphail, 1983; Hill, 1987) suggests that the flora is unlikely to be older than the (latest?) Late Oligocene. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
lithdescript: The fossils occur in a mudstone lens approximately 15 m long and about 1.5 m thick which has been exposed in a channel-cutting on the Central Plateau. The lens is overlain by about 2 m of basalt. \r\nThe plant fossils described by Macphail and Hill 1991 come from a mudstone exposed in the west wall of the Monpeelyata Canal which diverts water from the Ouse River into the Lake Echo hydroelectic impoundment. The exposure occurs directly next to the bridge on the Monpeelyata Canal service road. The mudstone lens forms part of a thin (<2 m?) concave lenticular sedimentary sequence that overlies Jurassic dolerite and is overlain by massive to vesicular, alkali olivine basalt. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)

The sediments are located in an old river valley at relatively low altitude (90 m above sea level), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
stratcomments: The fossil-bearing mudstone has been dated by palynological correlation by M. K. Macphail. He considers that the mudstone belongs to the lower Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone of Stover & Partridge, 1973 (hill & Bigwood, 1987). Macphail (in Hill 1987) suggested a Late Oligocene age for the flora.\r\nThe sediments are dated palynologically as Early Oligocene (Macphail et al. 1994) in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
lithdescript: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The lower unit is at least 2 m in depth and is composed of a very fine-grained dark grey mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils. mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils.\r\nAbove the organic layer which separates the two units the sediment changes suddenly to a coarser grained material composed of dark grey sands, once again rich in black organic material. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1989 & Hill and Carpenter, 1989 were recovered from the fluviatile sands of this place.

geology_comments: It is likely that the Little Rapid River deposit represents a Tertiary lake which has undergone a dramatic change in depositional regimes. The lower unit is characteristic of a low energy environment such as the centre of a lake with low stream input. Organic laminations would be the result of fluctuating stream flow (possibly seasonal), the plant matter most probably being derived from vegetation lining inflowing creeks and streams or from the lake edge itself.

stratcomments: The stratigraphy of Seymour Island is summarized by Macellari and Huber (Antarctic Journal, this issue; Campanian to ? Paleocene, Lopez de Bertodano and Sobral Formations) and by Zinsmeister and DeVries (Antarctic Journal, this issue; ? Paleocene to lower Oligocene, Seymour Island Group).
lithdescript: The Sobral Formation, which may be Maestrichtian to Paleocene in age, overlies the Lopez de Bertodano Formation in an apparently concordant fashion. It consists of up to 265 meters of somewhat coarser and more glauconitic silty sandstone, grading into fine-grained sandstones. Rounded concretions and concretionary horizons are frequent. Some beds are laterally continuous, but generally this formation shows a more pronounced lateral variation than the previous unit. The base of the Sobral Formation is a laterally continuous, 15-20-meter thick, dark brown, well-laminated to flaser-bedded silty mudstone which displays local channels. This moderately resistant bed produces a conspicuous positive break an the topography. A continuous, well-cemented, large-scale trough cross- bedded glauconitic sandstone appears at approximately 180 meters from the base of the Sobral. Above this, the sequence becomes more sandy, glauconitic, and occasionally yellow- stained, with increasingly abundant concretions and fossil wood (Macellari and Huber, 1982)
primary_reference: R. A. Askin and R. F. Fleming. 1982. Palynological investigations of Campanian to Lower Oligocene sediments on Seymour Island, Antarctic Peninsula. Antarctic Journal of the US 17(5):70-71

El perfil estudiado comprende un tramo de secuencia de unos 370 m de potencia, de los cuales los 120 inferiores pertenecen a la parte alta de la Fm. López de Bertodano y el resto a la Fm. Sobral.

Haciendo referencia a las edades la Fm. Lopez de Bertodano fue asignada en base a amonites ai Campaniano (OLIVERO. 1981) o Maastrichtiano (MACELLARI, 1985). EI contenido polínico en el caso de la Fm Lopez de Bertodano, la presencia de Grapnelispora evansii incluso en los términos cuspida[es de esta unidad, apoyaría la edad dada en base a amonites y descartaría la existencia de terrenos terciarios dentro de dicha formación por lo menos en la zona involucrada por la traza del perfil 3, a pesar de ello, en virtud de las pocas citas de esta espora hacen que ésto no tenga más que un caracter tentativo.
primary_reference: M. A. Baldoni and V. D. Barreda. 1986. Estudio palinológico de las formaciones López de Bertodano y Sobral, Isla Vicecomodoro Marambio, Antártida. Boletín del IG-USP, Serie Científica (17):89-98
geology_comments: La abundancia de fagáceas, formas desarrolladas actualmente en áreas de clima templado y húmedo como los Andes Patagónicos (Argentina), sugieren semejantes condiciones para las asociaciones vegetales existentes en los tiempos Cretacico superior - Paleoceno de la Isla Vicecomodoro Marambio.
collection_comments: Las muestras estudiadas fueron procesadas en el laboratorio palinológico del CIRGEO utilizando las técnicas convencionales de eliminación de carbonatos y silicatos seguidos por una suave oxidación en los casos en que fue necesario. Posteriormente se procedió a la separación con fluidos pesados y al filtrado por malla de diferentes diámetros quedando así aptas para su montaje. Los preparados microscópicos se hallan depositado en la palinoteca del nombrado centro bajo los números 693 a 716.

El perfil estudiado comprende un tramo de secuencia de unos 370 m de potencia, de los cuales los 120 inferiores pertenecen a la parte alta de la Fm. López de Bertodano y el resto a la Fm. Sobral.

Haciendo referencia a las edades la Fm. Lopez de Bertodano fue asignada en base a amonites ai Campaniano (OLIVERO. 1981) o Maastrichtiano (MACELLARI, 1985). EI contenido polínico en el caso de la Fm Lopez de Bertodano, la presencia de Grapnelispora evansii incluso en los términos cuspida[es de esta unidad, apoyaría la edad dada en base a amonites y descartaría la existencia de terrenos terciarios dentro de dicha formación por lo menos en la zona involucrada por la traza del perfil 3, a pesar de ello, en virtud de las pocas citas de esta espora hacen que ésto no tenga más que un caracter tentativo.
primary_reference: M. A. Baldoni and V. D. Barreda. 1986. Estudio palinológico de las formaciones López de Bertodano y Sobral, Isla Vicecomodoro Marambio, Antártida. Boletín del IG-USP, Serie Científica (17):89-98
geology_comments: La abundancia de fagáceas, formas desarrolladas actualmente en áreas de clima templado y húmedo como los Andes Patagónicos (Argentina), sugieren semejantes condiciones para las asociaciones vegetales existentes en los tiempos Cretacico superior - Paleoceno de la Isla Vicecomodoro Marambio.
collection_comments: Las muestras estudiadas fueron procesadas en el laboratorio palinológico del CIRGEO utilizando las técnicas convencionales de eliminación de carbonatos y silicatos seguidos por una suave oxidación en los casos en que fue necesario. Posteriormente se procedió a la separación con fluidos pesados y al filtrado por malla de diferentes diámetros quedando así aptas para su montaje. Los preparados microscópicos se hallan depositado en la palinoteca del nombrado centro bajo los números 693 a 716.

geogcomments: Road cutting approximately 0.5 km above and east of the Cethana Dam.
stratcomments:
According to Macphail (pers. comm.) the age of the flora is between Early Eocene and uppermost Oligocene (Hill, 1984).
Further palynological assessment suggests that the flora is likely to be in the Late Eocene to Oligocene range based on the high proportion of Nothofagus brassii-type and Phyllocladidites mawsonii pollen (Carpenter & Hill, 1988).
The palynoflora has been assigned to the early Oligocene by Macphail et al. 1994. The presence of Cyatheacidites annulatus provides a confident Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone (Stover and Partridge 1973) maximum age, but the upper age limits are less certain owing to possible diachronism in the times of extinction of accessory species such as Beaupreadites verrucosus, Granodiporites nebulosus and Triporopollenites ambiguus. (Hill et al. 2008)
lithdescript: The deposit unconformably overlies folded quartzose arenaceous (Moina Sandstone) meta-sediments. The fossiliferous rock is a creamy-yellow to light brown-grey laminated siltstone with alternations of thin sand layers. Fossils from Hill & Carpenter, 1988 were recovered from mudstone of the same locality.
primary_reference: R. J. Carpenter. 1991. Palaeovegetation and Environment at Cethana, Tasmania.
lithdescript.1: The deposit unconformably overlies folded quartzose arenaceous (Moina Sandstone) meta-sediments. The fossiliferous rock is a creamy-yellow to light brown-grey laminated siltstone with alternations of thin sand layers. Fossils from Hill & Carpenter, 1988 were recovered from mudstone of the same locality.
geology_comments: The fine laminated siltstone with terrestrial plant fragments indicates a low energy depositional environment such as a lake centre. The sand layers may indicate fluctuating stream inflow on the lake edges.\r\nThe Cethana deposit had an Early Oligocene altitude of about 300 m. It formed at a time for which there is evidence of regional glacial activity (Macphail et al. 1993), in Carpenter & Jordan, 1997.

geology_comments: Fine mudstone and clay rich in mummified leaves and probably represent deposition in cut-off branches of a meandering river system.

geogcomments: The fossiliferous sediment outcrops in a cutting situated on an abandoned logging road approximately 2 km south of the Little Rapid River.\r\nRoad cutting in the northwest of Tasmania, 35 km south of Smithton. The sediments are located in an old river valley at relatively low altitude (90 m above sea level), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
stratcomments: The fossil-bearing mudstone has been dated by palynological correlation by M. K. Macphail. He considers that the mudstone belongs to the lower Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone of Stover & Partridge, 1973 (hill & Bigwood, 1987). Macphail (in Hill 1987) suggested a Late Oligocene age for the flora.\r\nThe sediments are dated palynologically as Early Oligocene (Macphail et al. 1994) in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
lithdescript: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The lower unit is at least 2 m in depth and is composed of a very fine-grained dark grey mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils. mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils.\r\nAbove the organic layer which separates the two units the sediment changes suddenly to a coarser grained material composed of dark grey sands, once again rich in black organic material. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1989 & Hill and Carpenter, 1989 were recovered from the fluviatile sands of this place.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill and M. S. Pole. 1992. Leaf and Shoot Morphology of Extant Afrocarpus, Nageia and Retrophyllum (Podocarpaceae) Species, and Species with Similar Leaf Arrangement, from Tertiary Sediments in Australasia. Australian Systematic Botany 5(3):337-358

Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1989 & Hill and Carpenter, 1989 were recovered from the fluviatile sands of this place.
geology_comments: It is likely that the Little Rapid River deposit represents a Tertiary lake which has undergone a dramatic change in depositional regimes. The lower unit is characteristic of a low energy environment such as the centre of a lake with low stream input. Organic laminations would be the result of fluctuating stream flow (possibly seasonal), the plant matter most probably being derived from vegetation lining inflowing creeks and streams or from the lake edge itself.
collection_comments: Fossils collected by R. S. Hill from 1992 to 1998 (Guerin & Hill, 2003).

geogcomments: Deposit located in an abandoned tin mine approximately 7 km north of the village of Pioneer in north-eastern Tasmania (Pole, 1992).
stratcomments: The Hasties mudstone was more difficult to date precisely but probably belongs in the Lower Nothofagidites asperus zone. The presence of Nothofagidites falcatus and N. asperus sets the maximum age, while Aglaoreidia qualumis sets both maximum and minimum ages. The remaining taxa have wide stratigraphic ranges, but none fall outside the suggested Middle-Late Eocene age (Stover and Partridge 1973).
lithdescript: The plant remains described here come from a carbonaceous mud to slightly lignitic unit, 2 m thick, lying within several metres of poorly sorted quartzose gravel with poorly defined cross-bedding and well preserved fragments of wood (Pole, 1992).

geogcomments: Darling Plateau at West Dale, 76 km east southeast of Perth and 325 km west southwest of Beverley, Western Australia. The fossil-bearing outcrop lies about 270 m above sea level on the eastern slope of the drainage divide between the west-flowing Darkin and the east-flowing Dale Rivers. The Darkin River joins the Helena River and the Dale flows into the Avon-Swan system, both of which eventually flow west through the Darling escarpment to the Swan Coastal Plain. original Coodinate: 32°13.6'S, 116°36.2'E.
stratcomments: If the postulated sequence of events at West Dale is correct, then the upper age limit for the plant fossils in the siltstone layer would possibly be Oligocene. The lower limit is unknown, but is presumed to be within the Early Tertiary.
lithdescript: The fossil matrix is a yellowish-brown siltstone with inclusive small lenses of sand. The siltstone is fissile and the tabulate floaters produced from it split readily to reveal the fossil plants which have been preserved in iron oxides with some limonitic deterioration.
primary_reference: R. S. Hill and H. E. Merrifield. 1993. An Early Tertiary macroflora from West Dale, southwestern Australia. Alcheringa 17(4):285-326
lithdescript.1: The fossil matrix is a yellowish-brown siltstone with inclusive small lenses of sand. The siltstone is fissile and the tabulate floaters produced from it split readily to reveal the fossil plants which have been preserved in iron oxides with some limonitic deterioration.
geology_comments: The fine grain of the siltstone and the preservation of plant material by iron oxide replacement are consistent with low energy and anaerobic fossilisation conditions. The presence of sand suggests the siltstone was part of a sluggish river system, perhaps a billabong, but open to occasional direct discharge.

geogcomments: 2 km north-east of Anglesea. Clay lens of the new Block Two Site, c. 0.5 km from the lenses of the original mine, Christophel (1984).
stratcomments: The deposit is considered to be Upper Eocene (Christophel 1981) and recent palynological investigations (A. lithdescript: clay lens of the new Block Two Site, c. 0.5 km from the lenses of the original mine. Two laterally extensive fossiliferous lenses in the mudstones and unconsolidated sands unconformably overlying the brown coal of the Eastern View Formation occurs c. 70 m below the ground surface and extends c. 60 m laterally along the south-east face of the Block Two Site. The lens varies in thickness from 0.5 to 3.0 m.

geogcomments: The fossiliferous sediment outcrops in a cutting situated on an abandoned logging road approximately 2 km south of the Little Rapid River.\r\nRoad cutting in the northwest of Tasmania, 35 km south of Smithton. The sediments are located in an old river valley at relatively low altitude (90 m above sea level), in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
stratcomments: The fossil-bearing mudstone has been dated by palynological correlation by M. K. Macphail. He considers that the mudstone belongs to the lower Proteacidites tuberculatus Zone of Stover & Partridge, 1973 (hill & Bigwood, 1987). Macphail (in Hill 1987) suggested a Late Oligocene age for the flora.\r\nThe sediments are dated palynologically as Early Oligocene (Macphail et al. 1994) in Guerin & Hill, 2003.
lithdescript: The deposit is composed of two different lithological units, each corresponding with a separate environment of deposition. The lower unit is at least 2 m in depth and is composed of a very fine-grained dark grey mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils. mudstone characterised by many layers of black organic material containing macrofossils.\r\nAbove the organic layer which separates the two units the sediment changes suddenly to a coarser grained material composed of dark grey sands, once again rich in black organic material. Both upper and lower units are consolidated when dry but become plastic when wet. Fossils from Hill, 1989 & Hill and Carpenter, 1989 were recovered from the fluviatile sands of this place.

geology_comments: It is likely that the Little Rapid River deposit represents a Tertiary lake which has undergone a dramatic change in depositional regimes. The lower unit is characteristic of a low energy environment such as the centre of a lake with low stream input. Organic laminations would be the result of fluctuating stream flow (possibly seasonal), the plant matter most probably being derived from vegetation lining inflowing creeks and streams or from the lake edge itself.
collection_comments: Fossils collected by R. S. Hill from 1992 to 1998 (Guerin & Hill, 2003).

geogcomments: Approximately 1 km south of the southern shore of Lake Eyre South.
stratcomments: Based on palynological dating the Formation ranges in age from latest Paleocene to Middle Eocene (Alley, 1998).\r\nNelly Creek palynoflora correlates with the Lower Nothofagidites asperus Zone of Stover & Partridge (1973) and with the Proteacidites pachypolus Zone of Harris (1971), and the Nelly Creek flora is correlative with the floras at Maslin Bay and Golden Grove (Hiil & Christophel, 2001).
lithdescript: The deposit consists of sands, silts and grey, carbonaceous clays forming a portion of the bed of Nelly Creek. The deposit is restricted to the stream bed and is only accessible when little or no water is found in Nelly Creek (Hiil & Christophel, 2001).\r\nThe Eyre Formation consists largely of mature, pyritic, carbonaceous sand, that is often leached in outcrop, silt and gravel. Lignite and clay, sometimes with root horizons and leaf beds, are common. A diagnostic feature of the base of the unit is a polished gravel composed of resistant lithologies such as milky quartz, chert, jasper, agate, fossil wood and silcrete, with pebbles of basement rock in some localities (Alley, 1998).
primary_reference: R. S. Hill and D. C. Christophel. 2001. Two New Species of Dacrydium (Podocarpaceae) Based on Vegetative Fossils from Middle Eocene Sediments at Nelly Creek, South Australia. Australian Systematic Botany 14(2):193-205

The deposit is restricted to the stream bed and is only accessible when little or no water is found in Nelly Creek (Hiil & Christophel, 2001).\r\nThe Eyre Formation consists largely of mature, pyritic, carbonaceous sand, that is often leached in outcrop, silt and gravel. Lignite and clay, sometimes with root horizons and leaf beds, are common. A diagnostic feature of the base of the unit is a polished gravel composed of resistant lithologies such as milky quartz, chert, jasper, agate, fossil wood and silcrete, with pebbles of basement rock in some localities (Alley, 1998).
geology_comments: Locally, the formation was deposited in a meandering channel to floodplain environment and the carbonaceous (leaf-bearing) clay in backwater swamps and shallow lakes on the floodplain (Alley et al. 1996). The leaf-bearing sediments are only accessible when little or no water is present.

stratcomments: The Regatta Point mudstone was placed in the Malvacipollis diversus zone, based on the presence of Intratriporopollenites notabilis, Liliacidites lanceolatus, Polycolpites esobalteus, Proteacidites grandis, P. leightonii and Spinizonocolpites priminatus, which have their first appearance in the M. diversus zone. None of the species characteristic of the more recent Proteacidites asperopolus zone were present. Therefore the Regatta Point mudstone is of Early Eocene age.

geogcomments: The Monpeelyata deposit is exposed in a canal cut by the Hydro-Electric Commission to connect the two impoundments of Little Pine Lagoon and Lake Echo.
stratcomments: The sediments are regarded as probably late Oligocene or early Miocene age based on analysis of microflora and radiometric dates of closely associated basalts (Hill & Gibson, 1986).\r\nThe area has been dated using K-Ar analysis, the age range 23.6-21.8 Myr (Sutherland et al. 1973).These results agree with the palynological data, and an earliest Miocene age is therefore proposed for the Monpeelyata deposit, with the probable age falling within the period 21.8-23.6 Myr (M.K. Macphail, personal communication).\r\nThe age of Monpeelyata is based on a combination of palynological data and K-Ar dates on basalt flows in the area surrounding Great Lake. Both sets of data point to the Monpeelyata flora being no younger than earliest Miocene. The maximum age is less well defined although the absence of a large number of species found in Oligocene palynoflora in northern Tasmania (Hill & Macphail, 1983; Hill, 1987) suggests that the flora is unlikely to be older than the (latest?) Late Oligocene. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
lithdescript: The fossils occur in a mudstone lens approximately 15 m long and about 1.5 m thick which has been exposed in a channel-cutting on the Central Plateau. The lens is overlain by about 2 m of basalt. \r\nThe plant fossils described by Macphail and Hill 1991 come from a mudstone exposed in the west wall of the Monpeelyata Canal which diverts water from the Ouse River into the Lake Echo hydroelectic impoundment. The exposure occurs directly next to the bridge on the Monpeelyata Canal service road. The mudstone lens forms part of a thin (<2 m?) concave lenticular sedimentary sequence that overlies Jurassic dolerite and is overlain by massive to vesicular, alkali olivine basalt. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
primary_reference: M. K. Macphail, R. S. Hill, and S. M. Forsyth, P. M. Wells. 1991. A Late Oligocene Early Miocene cool climate flora in Tasmania. Alcheringa 15(2):87-106

The lens is overlain by about 2 m of basalt. \r\nThe plant fossils described by Macphail and Hill 1991 come from a mudstone exposed in the west wall of the Monpeelyata Canal which diverts water from the Ouse River into the Lake Echo hydroelectic impoundment. The exposure occurs directly next to the bridge on the Monpeelyata Canal service road. The mudstone lens forms part of a thin (<2 m?) concave lenticular sedimentary sequence that overlies Jurassic dolerite and is overlain by massive to vesicular, alkali olivine basalt. geology_comments: It is probable that the depositional environment was a shallow freshwater lake or tarn similar to the many alpine lakes which currently occur in the Tasmanian highlands (Hill 1988).\r\nAbundant remains of the freshwater hydrophyte Isoetes (Hill, 1988) and the fine grain size of the emergent sedimentary rock indicate a low energy depositional environment, probably a shallow pond, a sluggish river channel, or less likely a shallow, sheltered lake bay, subaerially exposed before or during lava extrusions. (Macphail and Hill, 1991)
taxonomy_comments: 830 podocarpaceous specimens.

geogcomments: Río Turbio Region, S. W. the Santa Cruz province. Carboniferous deposits.
stratcomments: Lower section of Cerro Dorotea Fm. was dated as Danian.
lithdescript: Sección Inferior: 43 m de areniscas gruesas con niveles conglomeráticos con restos de troncos y hojas de Fagáceas. 46 m de areniscas finas con restos de plantas de invertebrados. 110 m de areniscas con flora (arroyo Sta. Flavia) y bancos de conglomerados. En la mitad superior de este paquete es donde hallamos las arcillas carbonosas que contiene los palinomorfos que dan motivo a este estudio. Siguen después 90 m de areniscas y conglomerados con restos de moluscos entremezclados con fragmentos de plantas.
primary_reference: C. Freile. 1972. Estudio Palinológico de la Formación Cerro Dorotea (Maestrichtiano-Paleoceno) de la Provincia de Santa Cruz. I. Revista del Museo de la Plata (nueva serie), Sección Paleontología 6(38):39-63

Flavia) y bancos de conglomerados. En la mitad superior de este paquete es donde hallamos las arcillas carbonosas que contiene los palinomorfos que dan motivo a este estudio. Siguen después 90 m de areniscas y conglomerados con restos de moluscos entremezclados con fragmentos de plantas.
collection_comments: Conteos sobre 200 granos, en dos series de muestras, preparadas separadamente.\r\nThe preparation of the samples was carried out according to standard technique, with acid treatment (hydrochloric acid and hydrofluoric acid) and centrifugation for 24 hours. Both the microscope preparations and the residue are deposited in the palynological collection of the Paleobotanical Division of the Faculty of Natural Sciences. The observation of the material was performed using an Ortolux microscope from the same division, and the photomicrograph was taken with a Leika camera, using Kodak KB 14 and Duplo-Pan G film. The coordinates of the material are recorded in the laboratory under Ortolux number 626.478 of the Paleobotanical Division of the Faculty of Natural Sciences.

geogcomments: The site occurs in a road cutting only a few metres above sea level at Regatta Point, Macquarie Harbour.
stratcomments: The Regatta Point fossils are contained within transported blocks of sediment which have been dated by palynological correlation as Early or possibly Middle Pleistocene (Macphail et al. 1993). Dated as Late Pliocene-Early Pleistocene by Hill and Macphail, 1985; Wells & Hill, 1989.
lithdescript: The fossil occur in soft mudstone blocks situated in a glacifluvial outwash gravel above an Early Eocene mudstone. \r\nThe mudstone blocks are composed of quartz grains, black organic fragments,\r\nwhole plant structures and cream-coloured mud flakes all dispersed through a dark brown-grey mudstone matrix (Wells & Hill, 1989). Macrofossils from Jordan, 1997 were extracted from mudstone, siltstone and sandstone clasts within the gravels.
primary_reference: G. J. Jordan. 1995. Extinct conifers and conifer diversity in the Early Pleistocene of western Tasmania. Review of Palaeobotany and Palynology 84:375-387
lithdescript.1: The fossil occur in soft mudstone blocks situated in a glacifluvial outwash gravel above an Early Eocene mudstone. \r\nThe mudstone blocks are composed of quartz grains, black organic fragments,\r\nwhole plant structures and cream-coloured mud flakes all dispersed through a dark brown-grey mudstone matrix (Wells & Hill, 1989). Macrofossils from Jordan, 1997 were extracted from mudstone, siltstone and sandstone clasts within the gravels.
geology_comments: The blocks have been transported an unkwown distance from the original site of deposition. It is unlikely that they have travelled far, since they are large (1 m3), close together and very angular, with little sign of erosion.\r\n\r\nThe fine-grained nature of the sediment matrix indicates distal deposition in a low-energy environment such as a lake, river estuary or a shallow inland harbour such as the one existing there today (Wells & Hill, 1989).
collection_comments: Repository: Department of Plant Science at the University of Tasmania.\r\npollen count min. 400 identifiable pollen and spores (Jordan et al., 1995).
taxonomy_comments: Includes macrofossils and microfossils.

geogcomments: Exposure near the top of a roadside quarry.
stratcomments: On palynological evidence, Raine (1988) reported a Teurian (Paleocene) age for coal measures in the Kakahu area, assigning them to the PM3 palynological zone of Raine (1984). The base of this zone probably approximates the Cretaceous - Tertiary boundary while the upper limit may be Early Eocene. He noted that the leaf beds at this locality grade upwards into Bortonian (mid Eocene) marine strata.
primary_reference: M. Pole. 1997. Paleocene plant macrofossils from Kakahu, south Canterbury, New Zealand. Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand 27(3):371-400
time_overlap: Cenomanian, Turonian, Coniacian, Santonian, Campanian, Maastrichtian, Danian, Selandian, Thanetian, Ypresian
geology_comments: Wellman (1953) described the geology of the Kakahu area where coal measures containg plant macrofossils unconformably overlie metamorphosed Torlesse sediments (mainly Mesozoic) at the base of a marine sequence. The coal beds and much of the overlying marine sediments are here interpreted as belonging to the Onekakara Group of Carter (1988), covering "paralic and shallow shelf and ramp sediments deposited during a Late Cretaceous - Oligocene marine transgression, caused by flexural subsidence of the eastern New Zealand margin during post-rift cooling" The plant fossils come from his Taratu Fm, equivalent to the Broken River Formation of Field & Browne (1986).

stratcomments: The Loncoche Formation (Campanian to early Maastrichtian, Upper Cretaceous) is the basal unit of the Malargüe Group.
lithdescript: In this section, the Loncoche Fm. is composed of clayey, silty, and sandy beds, with some gypsum and marls interbedded, integrated into four depositional facies associations (Parras et al. 2001; Previtera and González Riga 2008).
primary_reference: O. H. Papú. 2002. Nueva microflora de edad maastichtiana en la localidad de Calmu-Co, sur de Mendoza, Argentina. Ameghiniana 39(4):415-426

geology_comments: Parras et al. (1998) and Parras and Griffin (2013) interpreted the depositional environment of the area (south of Mendoza) as fluvial to deltaic, with a few lacustrine episodes under a sporadic marine influence, for the lower and middle part of the Loncoche Fm.

zone: T. lilliei and T. longus zones
stratcomments:
The stratigraphic framework and dinoflagellate cyst succession have been summarized for the Campanian to Paleocene of Seymour Island (Askin, 1988a).

The lower and upper parts of the Seymour Island late Campanian to Maastrichtian succession (units 1-9 of López de Bertodano Formation) correspond respectively to the T. lilliei and T. longus Zones of southeastern Australia (Stover and Evans, 1973; Helby et al., 1987). Both parts correlate with the PM2 Zone of South Island, New Zealand (Raine, 1984).
lithdescript: The Formation consists predominantly of poorly consolidated, grey sandy silts with mud-rich units in the lower part, some fine-grained, often calcareous sandstone beds throughout the section, and glauconite beds in the uppermost part.
primary_reference: R. A. Askin. 1990. Campanian to Paleocene spore and pollen assemblages of Seymour Island, Antarctica. Review of Palaeobotany and Palynology (65):105-113
lithdescript.1: The Formation consists predominantly of poorly consolidated, grey sandy silts with mud-rich units in the lower part, some fine-grained, often calcareous sandstone beds throughout the section, and glauconite beds in the uppermost part.
geology_comments: Most of this succession was deposited in low energy, nearshore marine paleoenvironments. A regression, beginning near the end of the Cretaceous, changed shallow shelf conditions in most of the López de Bertodano Formation to inshore/estuarine depositional environments in the basal Danian beds (member/"unit" 10 of López de Bertodano Formation).

stratcomments:

collection_comments: Palynomorphs discussed here are from approximately 500 outcrop samples in measured sections through the upper Campanian, Maastrichtian and Paleocene López de Bertodano and Sobral Formations.

geogcomments: The study area is located between two zones: 1, Estancia Laguna Salada (51º 10’ 49’’S, 72º 17’ 23’’O), Cancha Carrera, near Argentina-Chile boundary; and 2, Estancia San José (51º 35’ 11’’S, 72º 24’ 23’’O), Río Turbio zone, Santa Cruz province.
stratcomments: A preliminary palynological analysis of Cretaceous sequences near the study area (Povilauskas et al., 2006; Povilauskas & Guler, 2008) suggested a marginal marine depositional environment close to the shoreline, and an age around the Maastrichtian–late Maastrichtian (Povilauskas 2011).
lithdescript: The Monte Chico Formation is composed of fine to medium sandstones, light brown to reddish brown and greenish gray in color, partly calcareous, with abundant dark gray concretions containing a fossil invertebrate megafauna; mudstones, limonites with coquina-like interbeds, and conglomerates bearing megafossils (Malumián & Panza, 1996).
primary_reference: L. K. Povilauskas. 2010. Palinología del entorno cretácico/paleógeno del SO de la provincia de Santa Cruz: significado estratigráfico y paleoambiental. Universidad Nacional de La Plata. Facultad de Ciencias Naturales y Museo de La Plata
lithdescript.1: The Monte Chico Formation is composed of fine to medium sandstones, light brown to reddish brown and greenish gray in color, partly calcareous, with abundant dark gray concretions containing a fossil invertebrate megafauna; mudstones, limonites with coquina-like interbeds, and conglomerates bearing megafossils (Malumián & Panza, 1996).
geology_comments: As a result, it is interpreted that the entire unit was deposited under a marginal coastal regime, probably shallow, under warm and at least locally humid climatic conditions (Povilauskas, 2013).
collection_comments: Repository: MPM-MP, Museo Regional Provincial “Padre Manuel Jesús Molina”, Río Gallegos, Provincia de Santa Cruz, Argentina.\r\nPalynological extraction was carried out following conventional physical and chemical extraction methods for palynology (HCl-HF), and the resulting residue was filtered using +10 and +25 micron meshes. The final preparations were mounted in glycerin jelly. Specimens were studied using a Leitz Wetzlar Germany microscope and an Olympus BX51 from the Paleopalynology Section, and were photographed using both a transmitted light optical microscope and a scanning electron microscope (SEM) at the Argentine Museum of Natural Sciences 'Bernardino Rivadavia'. For photographic documentation of the specimens, a Nikon E4500 digital camera was used. The semi-natural classification system proposed by Pocock (1962) was followed, using morphotaxa at the genus and species level.

lithdescript: The Monte Chico Formation is composed of fine to medium sandstones, light brown to reddish brown and greenish gray in color, partly calcareous, with abundant dark gray concretions containing a fossil invertebrate megafauna; mudstones, limonites with coquina-like interbeds, and conglomerates bearing megafossils (Malumián & Panza, 1996).
